Acid-Washed Knit Beanie (Rolled Cuff)#

A ribbed knit beanie in dark teal gone patchy and pale from repeated exposure to Shelf acid-rain, the color now a mottled map of where the rain hit hardest. Rolled cuff is double-thick for ear coverage in lake-effect wind. A small repair darn sits near the crown where the knit snagged on something and tore through.

Adisa Handwoven Pullover#

Made by Adisa Okonkwo-Brennan, a single artisan working out of a fourth-floor studio in the Tier 3 Havenwood district, these pullovers are woven on a traditional floor loom using a blend of West African kente strip-weaving technique and Nordic colorwork structure. Each pullover is assembled from strips of hand-woven fabric joined in a way that makes the seams a design element rather than a flaw. The color combinations are Adisa's own — warm golds and deep indigos alongside unexpected interventions of forest green or rust. No two are identical. The fabric is a wool-linen blend that has a pleasant roughness when new and breaks in to something close to linen-soft over time.

Adisa sells through a small waiting list and occasionally through a Tier 3 design collective market. Prices are firm and non-negotiable. The pullovers have found their way onto people across tiers — Tier 2 buyers who saved for months, Tier 4 buyers who appreciate the provenance, and one documented Tier 5 Spire resident who keeps it as their 'real clothes' for private evenings. Adisa doesn't care who buys them as long as the list stays moving.

Aldren & Moss Classic Oxford#

A full-brogue oxford in deep mahogany synth-leather with a hand-buffed finish that holds its shine through a full workday. The sole is thin-profile rubber with micro-tread, almost invisible from the side. Nothing flashy — just a very well-made shoe that signals you've been around long enough to know what good looks like.

Aldren & Moss Handsewn Longwing Brogue#

Cut from a single hide of genuine cowhide — the real thing, not cultured — and hand-welted by artisans at Aldren & Moss's Tier 4 atelier in the Meridian Garment Quarter. The full brogue medallion and wingtip stitching are done by eye, no two pairs identical. Comes in deep oxblood or aged cognac.

Worn by senior corporate attorneys, old-money Tier 4 professionals, and anyone who wants to signal they bought something that will outlast them. The leather smell alone marks you as someone who spent real money.

Aldren Everyday Chino Short#

Aldren Packmule Utility Cargo Pant#

Generous straight-fit cargo pants with an almost absurd number of pockets — ten total, including two drop-leg side pockets secured with both button and zip, two hidden interior thigh channels, and a sealed rear document pocket. Built from a mid-weight canvas-cotton blend in tan, olive, or dark navy.

Favored by field technicians, medics, and anyone whose job requires having the right thing in the right place immediately. The drop-leg pockets are the signature feature — they sit lower than standard cargo pockets, keeping bulk off the hip and making deep storage accessible while seated. Looks utilitarian. Is utilitarian.

Ashgrain Tunnel Runner's Rig#

A head-to-toe survival layering system built for the underground transit tunnels and acid-washed overpass corridors of the Shelf. The base is a long-sleeve compression shirt in faded charcoal, fabric pilled and stress-creased at the shoulders from years of pack-wearing, with a cracked rubber collar seal at the neck — originally designed to interface with a hazmat hood, now just a relic that keeps acid mist off the throat. Over it sits a zip-front work vest in rusted olive canvas, every pocket reinforced with mismatched industrial webbing; the chest pocket holds a melted-edge transit card and a wedge of self-repair tape. The outer shell is a hip-length anorak in stained ash-gray, the hood lined with salvaged thermal mylar that crinkles when it moves. Seams along the left shoulder have been restitched three times in different thread colors — black, then tan, now a bright industrial orange that cuts across the gray like a scar. Trousers are heavy-gauge charcoal cargo pants with knee panels cut from conveyor belt rubber, stitched flat for crawling through duct access. The right thigh pocket is stuffed; the left is patched with a strip of Tenex sealant tape over a tear that never fully healed. Boots are thick-soled black work boots resoled with layered salvage rubber, the uppers cracked and sealed with weatherstrip compound, laces replaced with braided comms wire. A salvaged neural port cap — chrome, scuffed, clearly pulled from a discarded cyberware kit — sits clipped to the vest collar as a clasp, non-functional but worn like a badge.

Ashveil Duskwalk Crowd-Runner Rig#

Built for the runner who needs to disappear into a Tier 2-3 crowd and stay there for hours, this rig leads with a structured overshirt in deep forest green with a subtle woven texture — wide enough in the shoulders to conceal a subdermal rig, loose enough in the torso to break the silhouette of body armor. The overshirt has six interior pockets arranged in a deliberate pattern: two at chest height for flat storage, two mid-torso with reinforced magnetic closures for weapon retention, and two low-hip for tools or extraction gear. The back panel is a single sheet of scanner-resistant thermal-baffled fabric that reads as a normal cotton blend to passive scanners. Beneath it sits a dark teal long-sleeve base layer in breathable synth-silk with BCI-port access cuts at both temples and the nape of the neck, sealed with thin magnetic flaps when not in use. The trousers are a straight-leg dark navy workwear twill with hidden waistband storage, articulated knees, and a continuous internal channel along the right thigh for a blade or slim tool. Footwear is a mid-top athletic shoe in muted olive-grey with a split-toe last to accommodate digitigrade or wide geneware feet — the sole has a vibration-dampening layer that kills footstep resonance on metal floors. A slim wrap scarf in dark rust-orange doubles as a face cover, signal-blocking layer when doubled, or an arm sling in an emergency.

Ashveil Splitback Recon Ghost Rig#

Built for prolonged observation work in mid-density urban environments, this rig prioritizes stillness over movement — it's made to be worn for eight hours in a transit corridor, a market stall queue, or a service corridor without drawing a second look. The anchor piece is an anorak-style pullover in muted sand-ochre with subtle vertical stripe detail, a pattern common enough in Circuit-level workwear to register as background noise to any human observer or basic pattern-recognition surveillance. The anorak's hood is structured with internal wire framing that shapes to block facial recognition from above and side angles simultaneously, collapsing flat when not needed. A chest harness worn beneath the anorak — visible only when the zipper is opened — carries a modular tool rack: four interchangeable pouches that accept everything from a compact sidearm to a drone relay unit. The base layer is a long-sleeved thermal shirt in deep slate with a BCI-port collar notch at the rear nape, accommodating standard neural jack access without requiring the anorak to be removed. Trousers are straight-cut in medium grey with reinforced cuffs, an internal wire-routing sleeve along the right leg for aug-power, and three hidden waistband pockets accessible from inside the waistband only. Footwear is a low-profile athletic-style shoe in off-white with dark grey accent — the deliberate cleanliness of the shoes against the worn anorak reads as aspirational Tier 2, the universal human story of someone keeping one thing nice.

Ashveil Tunnel Runner's Compressed Rig#

Designed — if that word applies to something assembled from desperation and ingenuity — for moving fast through the Shelf's sub-infrastructure tunnels. The core piece is a long-sleeved base layer in matte charcoal, cut close to the body and treated with a rubberized coating along the forearms and shoulders for sliding through tight passages without tearing. Over it sits a sleeveless tactical vest, originally a Vantablack surplus piece with the branding sliced off and replaced with hand-stitched patches of various gray and black fabrics. Sixteen pockets of various sizes distribute weight evenly across the torso — some sealed with original magnetic closures still functioning, others sewn shut with fishing line, others left open for fast access. Trousers are skintight reinforced leggings in dark charcoal with articulated knee panels cut from a yoga mat and stitched in — ugly but effective padding. Over the thighs, a pair of salvaged thigh pockets are strapped directly to the legs with nylon webbing. The shoes are flat-soled, thin, and hand-repaired: originally a Patchwork Runner Low, now barely recognizable under layers of rubber adhesive patches and re-lacing with paracord. The face is partially covered by a wrap of dark gray filter cloth — not a proper respirator, but better than breathing raw tunnel air. A salvaged chrome forearm plate from a junked augmentation rig is strapped to the left forearm as a makeshift shield and tool surface, its exposed circuit traces long dead but the alloy still hard.

Aurelian & Co. Poplin Dress Shirt#

Aurelian & Co. is the kind of Tier 5 label that doesn't advertise — you either know it or you don't, and if you need to ask, the answer is probably not yet. The Poplin Dress Shirt is made from a long-staple Egyptian-analog cotton grown in controlled biofarms in the southern corridor and woven to a thread count that produces a fabric so smooth it has a faint luminosity in good light. The fit is cut close through the chest and tapers to the waist without becoming uncomfortable, and the collar is a semi-spread that works with or without a tie. French cuffs are standard.

The buttons are real shell — the kind that takes two months to source and another month to cut. The stitching is done by a team of twelve in a workshop above a Tier 4 district that Aurelian & Co. has occupied since the building was residential. Each shirt is numbered at the interior placket and registered to the buyer. It comes in white, off-white, and one blue so pale it reads as white in dim light. It does not wrinkle because people who wear this shirt do not allow circumstances that would wrinkle it.

Aurelis Spire Cashmere Blazer#

A single-breasted two-button blazer in a double-faced cashmere that falls somewhere between suiting fabric and a very structured sweater — it holds its shape immaculately while feeling like nothing you've worn before. The construction is half-canvased, built by hand in Aurelis's Spire-district atelier. Patch pockets on a blazer at this price point is an intentional statement of studied informality. It's also worn to the kinds of events where the room knows exactly what everything costs and that's the entire point. The distinction between those two rooms is what separates the actually wealthy from the aspirationally wealthy.

Aurelius & Strand Thermal Overcoat#

Aurelius & Strand is a Tier 5 tailor operating from a single atelier on the upper floors of a Spire commercial tower, accepting clients by referral only. Their Thermal Overcoat is a floor-length piece in a double-faced cashmere-wool that falls with the kind of weight that makes movement feel deliberate. The exterior is available in three colors — deep charcoal, ivory, and a midnight blue that is almost but not quite black — and the interior face, which shows at the collar and lapel turn, is a contrasting cream or dove grey. Embedded in the chest lining is a passive thermal regulation mesh — not advertised, not explained in any documentation, simply present — that maintains a stable microclimate around the torso across a wide range of external temperatures. The wearer stays comfortable from a heated boardroom to an outdoor arrival platform without visible adjustment. This is a jacket for people who cannot afford to be seen to be cold. In the Spire, discomfort is a form of vulnerability, and Aurelius & Strand charges accordingly for its elimination.

Aurelius Collective Linen Dress Shirt#

Aurelius Collective is a small-batch label operating out of a rented studio in Tier 3 Milwaukee-South, run by a designer named Priya Osei-Nakamura whose background spans both tailoring and structural engineering. The linen dress shirt is their flagship piece — a spread-collar button-front cut slightly longer than standard, designed to be worn tucked or half-tucked with the same proportional integrity. The linen is a Japanese-mill blend that has a natural slub texture and softens dramatically after washing. Available in off-white, a warm terracotta, and a dusty sage.

Seam allowances are generous enough that a tailor can take it in without destroying the garment. Axgrip Facilities Maintenance Crew Set#

The daily working dress of an M88 building and infrastructure maintenance worker — the people who keep Circuit's residential blocks, transit hubs, and mid-level commercial buildings from falling apart. The outer layer is a zip-front work jacket in medium grey synth-fleece with a water-resistant outer shell laminate, warm enough for crawlspace and rooftop work in M88's variable climate. The left chest carries an embroidered patch for the maintenance contractor — in this case, Axgrip Facilities Group, a mid-tier Circuit services company whose logo is a stylized wrench in black and yellow. The jacket's right sleeve has a full-length aug-accommodation channel zip from shoulder to cuff, opening flat to allow a full chrome arm to be inserted or removed without undressing; the seam is double-stitched with reinforced stress points. Beneath is a yellow high-vis long-sleeved work shirt, the collar worn open, a BCI sync port visible at the base of the neck where the shirt's collar is cut with a notched relief.

Work trousers are charcoal heavy-canvas with articulated knees, six external pockets, and a hammer loop on the right thigh. A padded kneeling patch is sewn into the inner knee. Boots are lace-up mid-height in dark brown oiled leather, composite-toed, with a side-zip assist and a chunky rubber lug sole for grip on wet floors, ladder rungs, and rooftop membrane. The worker carries a worn canvas tool bag over one shoulder, patched at the bottom corner with adhesive synth-fabric. A yellow hard hat is clipped to the bag strap when not worn. Safety glasses with clear lenses hang from the jacket's front zipper pull. The whole set is anonymous in the best Circuit way — this person belongs in the building, and nobody looks twice.

Axiom Defense Concepts Sentinel Vest#

The Sentinel is a tactical soft-armor vest sold openly to licensed security personnel and, with the right documentation, to civilians. It looks like a structured workwear vest — multiple cargo pockets on the exterior in a flat coyote tan or urban charcoal, adjustable side panels, a drag handle at the back collar that most buyers remove because it draws attention. What it doesn't look like, from the outside, is a Level IIIA ballistic vest, which is what it is. The panels are ceramic-composite laminate sandwiched between the outer shell and an inner moisture-wicking mesh. It runs warm.

Private security contractors, licensed personal protection details, and a significant number of Tier 2 and Tier 3 civilians who live or work in contested zones wear these. The Shelf has stolen versions — usually older models with degraded panels that may or may not still test to spec. Axiom Defense Concepts is a corponation subsidiary that makes the bulk of its money in municipal security contracts; the Sentinel is their civilian-market product, priced to be accessible enough that liability questions stay manageable.

Axiom Defense Solutions Thermal Stealth Cloak#

This is not clothing. It is a wearable system. The Axiom ThermoCloak is a full-length hooded garment constructed from a phase-change metamaterial that actively disrupts thermal signature — wearing it, you appear on infrared as background noise. The outer surface can be set to passive environmental matching (not true invisibility, but significant visual disruption at range in low light). Battery life is eight hours active. The fabric is stiff at the edges and moves like a very heavy coat. It weighs four kilograms.

Axiom Defense Solutions is a Corponation-tier manufacturer, and this item is technically export-controlled — civilian purchase requires a Tier 4 security clearance or a corporate sponsorship letter. In practice, maybe one in ten buyers has the paperwork. The rest acquired theirs through the grey market, which Axiom tolerates because it keeps prices high and demand mysterious. Operators, fixers, corp security, and occasionally very serious criminals wear these. You do not buy this coat because it looks good.

Axis Meridian Corporate Rain Shell#

Brackwater Dye Cropped Hoodie#

A cropped pullover hoodie in a heavyweight French terry cotton-synth blend, dyed using an acid-wash process that produces organic, unrepeatable streaks of color — each one genuinely unique. They sell at market stalls, through a few sympathetic Tier 2 boutiques, and via a rotating contact list. The hoodie has become a minor status signal in Shelf-adjacent street culture: you know where to find it, or you don't.

Calder & Rhys Wool Trenchcoat#

A double-breasted wool trench in the classic tradition — belted, storm-flapped, with deep slash pockets and a half-lining in printed silk-analog. The belt almost always goes untied, draped rather than cinched. It reads as polished and understated, which is exactly the point.

Caldero Patchwork Layered Tank#

A Shelf staple assembled from salvaged textile scraps — panels of faded corporate workwear fabric stitched alongside strips of what was once a West African kente-print garment, a section of silver-gray thermal lining, and a band of heavy denim along one shoulder. No two Caldero tanks are identical because there is no Caldero — it's a street name for the guy on the Tier 1 market stall at the corner of Caldero and 9th who sews these by hand from whatever comes in that week. Shelf kids wear these under everything, or alone in summer, and the layered construction means there's always a pocket sewn somewhere unexpected — inside the kente panel, under the denim patch. It's not fashionable in any conventional sense, but on the Shelf it reads as resourceful, and resourceful is respected.

Cinderblock Nightwatch Wrap Set#

Built for low-visibility, low-movement work — the kind of watching that happens in doorways and on broken catwalks at 03:00. The foundation is a thermal long-sleeve base in charcoal heather, heavily pilled from repeated washing in whatever water is available, the neck stretched wide and re-hemmed with a doubled strip of elastic salvaged from a Pragma Systems base layer. Over this is a structured wrap-jacket in a deep, muted rust-brown — originally a single-piece garment, now split at the left side seam and re-closed with a row of mismatched pressure snaps that allow rapid removal or ventilation adjustment. The wrap folds across the chest and ties with a wide obi-style sash in faded indigo, its ends frayed to loose threads that the wearer has stopped cutting. The sash carries two flat pockets stitched directly onto it — one holding a folded emergency mylar sheet, one with a broken-seam closure holding a small medkit. The lower half is loose trousers in near-black canvas, hem-gathered at the ankle with salvaged elastic so they don't snag on debris, the left thigh bearing a large iron-on acid-shield patch in matte gray. Footwear is a low boot in cracked synthetic suede, the toe cap reinforced with a strip of steel salvaged from a junction box cover, riveted in place with hardware-store bolts. The head covering is a wide, flat-crown wrap cap in washed linen the color of old concrete, its brim stiffened with a strip of reclaimed wire sewn into the hem. The whole palette — rust, indigo shadow, charcoal, near-black — is dark enough to disappear in Shelf shadows but not so uniform as to read as tactical.

Circuit Ghost Wrap#

A look built for moving unseen through the Shelf's surveillance gaps and contested corridors. The base is a close-fitting long-sleeve in matte black moisture-wicking jersey, worn thin at the elbows, with a dead neural port interface sewn into the left collar — salvaged from a discarded BCI unit, non-functional but kept as a ward or trophy. Over it hangs a deconstructed puffer vest, the insulation long since redistributed unevenly so it sits flat in some panels and bunched in others, creating an unintentionally textured silhouette. The outer shell of the vest is coated in a peeling anti-reflective treatment that still works in low light. Slim straight-leg trousers in dark grey ripstop are belted with a length of doubled industrial webbing, the buckle a salvaged cargo clip. Three patch pockets run down the right thigh, each sealed with hook-and-loop closures worn almost to smoothness. Feet are wrapped in thin compression socks under low-profile sneakers with thick gum soles — the uppers re-glued at least twice, the toe cap reinforced with a strip of adhesive rubber. A long rectangular scarf in faded indigo cotton, washed to near-grey, is wound once around the neck and tucked into the vest. The hood of a destroyed jacket — just the hood, separated from its original garment — is clipped to the back collar of the vest with two carabiners, deployable in seconds.

Coldframe Quickshift Night Operative Set#

Bottoms are close-fit dark olive tech trousers with a thigh-holster integration on the right leg, a digitigrade gusset option built into the seat and thigh for gene-modified runners, and silent-edge hem cuffs that don't rasp on surfaces when crawling. Footwear is a matte black low-boot with memory-foam split sole, ankle wrap closure with no metallic hardware, and a recessed toe cap.

Coldpatch Elder Coat & Walk Set#

A full-length greatcoat in what was once a deep charcoal wool blend, now faded to a complex mix of grays and near-browns from years of acid rain, hand-washing, and sun exposure in the Shelf's filtered, dirty light. The coat falls to mid-calf and was clearly once a higher-tier garment — the construction quality beneath the damage is visible in the structured shoulders, the deep lapels, and the deliberate drape. It has been repaired so extensively that the repairs have become its primary visual identity: the left shoulder sports a large patch in rubberized olive canvas, its edges sealed with silver-gray self-repair tape folded into a clean border; the right sleeve carries three sequential patch repairs in progressively darker fabrics — charcoal, then near-black, then a strip of industrial gray rubber — recording years of acid-sleeve damage. The lining is entirely replaced, now a salvaged thermal blanket material in reflective silver, visible at the hem and collar as a glinting inner layer. The coat is belted with a wide leather strap that has been broken and re-stitched twice, the repair points marked by darker color where the leather was wetted and recured. Beneath the coat, a heavyweight turtleneck in faded ash marled knit sits close to the body, its ribbing loose at the collar from stretching but intact everywhere else. Wide-leg trousers in washed near-black canvas carry side-seam pockets and a reinforced seat. Footwear is a tall boot, resoled so many times the sole is now nearly an inch thick with layered rubber, the upper a patchwork of original leather and replacement panels in synthetic suede, the whole thing treated with a heavy waterproofing compound that gives it a waxy, uneven finish. A wide-brim hat in felted gray, its crown creased and its brim slightly warped but functional, completes the silhouette. The hat carries a single ornament: a small, carefully-polished piece of chrome scrap — possibly from a salvaged aug-component — pinned to the band.

Coldseam Night Watcher's Kit#

Night watch on the Shelf is informal, unglamorous, and necessary — someone has to sit the perimeter of a squat block or community shelter through the cold hours, watching for raiders, Corponation enforcement sweeps, and the slower threats. This outfit is optimized for stillness, warmth, and not being seen. The outer layer is a long hooded coat in near-black charcoal, the fabric a dense synthetic weave with a matte finish that absorbs rather than reflects available light — not a designed stealth coating, just a fabric that happens to work that way, likely cut from industrial blackout curtaining. The hood is deep and structured, holding its shape when raised, with a drawstring that cinches it to a narrow opening around the face. The coat's interior has been lined with panels of salvaged thermal batting, unevenly distributed — thicker at the torso and upper arms, thinner at the forearms for dexterity. Beneath the coat, a mid-layer pullover in dark heather gray sits over a thermal base layer in faded black; the pullover's cuffs are cut long and folded back, providing extra wrist coverage when unrolled. Trousers are close-cut in dark gray, with cargo pockets at the outer thighs — both sealed with friction-closure strips rather than zippers, to minimize noise. The boots are soft-soled mid-calf, the upper in cracked matte black synthetic leather, the sole a thick rubber compound that has been scraped smooth on the outer edge for silence on metal grating. Around the neck, a face wrap in dark charcoal — a long tube of fabric that can be pulled up to cover nose and mouth or worn loose. Fingerless gloves in worn dark leather leave the fingertips free; the right glove's index finger has been cut shorter than the others, exposing the tip of a cybernetic finger — matte black, clearly older-generation chrome, the joint slightly audible when flexed. A small battered earpiece sits in the left ear, the cord disappearing under the collar.

Coldseam Patched Occasion Suit — Shelf Best#

A two-piece suit assembled from mismatched fabric lots — the jacket a dark charcoal synth-wool, the trousers a slightly lighter black that has faded to near-gray at the knees. Both pieces have been let out and taken in multiple times; the evidence is visible in the seam lines if you look. The lapels are hand-pressed with something waxy, probably a bar of market soap, and hold their shape for a few hours before relaxing. The jacket's right sleeve has a careful patch at the elbow, stitched in a thread that is close but not quite matching.

On the Shelf, this is what you wear to your cousin's tier-certification hearing, to a funeral, to the one job interview that might mean something. It is clean. That matters more than anything else. People who wear this suit understand that being clean and pressed in a Tier 1 environment requires real effort and real sacrifice, and other Shelf residents recognize that effort immediately.

Crestline Selvedge Henley#

Crucible Fab-Floor Apprentice Daily Rig#

The standard daily kit for apprentice-grade workers on Crucible Industries' fabrication floors — one step below full technician, assigned to feed lines, operate basic presses, and assist with materials handling. The centerpiece is a flame-resistant coverall in Crucible's corporate deep red, overlaid with charcoal grey panels at the thighs and chest for reinforcement. The Crucible triangular logo is heat-bonded in silver on the upper back and left chest; a name patch in white sits above the right breast. The coverall's left sleeve has an aug channel — a velcro-and-snap seam that allows the sleeve to be peeled back or removed entirely for workers with forearm chrome, a mandatory accommodation on all Crucible fab-floor issue since the 2189 labor compact. The collar is high-cut with a chin guard snap for respirator attachment. Beneath the coverall, a heat-dispersing base layer in light grey manages thermal output from proximity to active machinery. Safety boots are Crucible-issued Penrose Weld Boots — steel-shank, heat-resistant sole, composite toe. A hard-shell safety helmet in the same deep red carries a flip-down UV-filter visor and a small rear port for BCI hard-line connection to the floor network. Insulated synth-leather work gloves clip to the coverall's chest ring when not in use.

Apprentices often mark their helmets with small stickers or hand-scratched tallies tracking shift counts toward their journeyman certification — an unofficial tradition the floor supervisors quietly tolerate. The coverall's deep red marks them instantly as Crucible property in motion through Circuit's streets, which carries both the protection of corponation affiliation and the occasional hostility from workers employed by rival fabricators.

Crucible HeavyWorks Maintenance Jumpsuit#

The HeavyWorks jumpsuit is what Crucible issues to the workers who keep the city's physical infrastructure running — furnace operators, crane riggers, pipeline maintenance crews, and the Tier 2 workforce that moves through Meridian 88's foundry districts and fabrication zones. The shell is a flame-retardant polyaramid composite reinforced at the knee, elbow, and shoulder with ceramic-fiber impact padding. Chrome arm augments fit cleanly through the articulated sleeve design, and the collar is cut low enough to avoid interference with common neck-port hardware. Crucible workers often personalize their jumpsuits heavily — patches, stitched names, local union insignia — and the company has an official policy of tolerating this as long as retroreflective markings remain unobscured. The jumpsuit is durable enough that some workers pass them down through families, three generations wearing the same shell with accumulated patches.

Crucible Investiture Ceremonial Robe — Ops Director#

Crucible's Investiture Robe for Operations Director appointments is produced internally by a small ceremonial fabrication team within the Crucible manufacturing complex. The robe is heavy — deliberately so — constructed from a layered heat-resistant formal weave in Crucible's signature deep iron-gray with copper and char-orange trim. The trim is real copper thread, not synthetic, sourced from Crucible's own smelting operations. The robe's weight is understood as symbolic: the new director is taking on something substantial. The front panel is embossed with Crucible's foundry mark in raised copper thread, and the lining is stamped with the appointee's name, date, and the names of the witnesses to the ceremony.

The robe is not worn again after the investiture. It is folded, sealed in a fabricated case, and presented to the new director as a permanent record of the appointment. Some directors display it; others store it. A very small number have sold theirs, which is not technically prohibited but is understood within Crucible culture as a significant statement about one's relationship to the company.

Crucible Investiture Formal Robe#

Crucible's corponation investiture robe is issued to employees achieving Division Principal rank or higher — a structured, floor-length garment in industrial charcoal and deep copper, the colors drawn from Crucible's founding charter documents. The outer layer is a heavy woven textile with a matte finish, its surface embedded with Crucible's operational insignia in raised metallic thread visible only under direct light. The lining is copper-tone silk-analog, smooth against chrome augments, with reinforced openings at the forearms and a structured hood that can be raised for ceremonial occasions. The garment is not sold — it is issued, registered to the recipient's personnel file, and formally returned upon departure from the corponation (or recovered from their estate).

The robe's weight is deliberate — approximately 2.3 kilograms — designed to be physically felt during the ceremony of investiture. Crucible's internal culture prizes the tangible, the built, the heavy. The robe communicates this. Investiture ceremonies are held in Crucible's foundry-floor event halls, where the ambient heat and sound of the manufacturing operation continue in the background. The robe is designed to perform dignity in that environment without looking out of place.

Crucible Loyalty Tattoo Overlay#

A semi-permanent dermal overlay — not ink, but a thin biocompatible film applied to the skin — displaying Crucible Genomics' loyalty insignia. The overlay changes in complexity with employee tenure: simple geometric patterns at five years, intricate circuit-like designs at ten, and a full sleeve of interlocking forge symbols at twenty. The overlay fades if not renewed annually at a Crucible facility.

The overlay is technically optional. In practice, employees who don't display loyalty markings find their advancement opportunities quietly limited. The annual renewal requirement ensures that former employees lose their markings — Crucible's way of saying you belong to them, or you don't.

Crucible Shift Floor General Ops Uniform#

The everyday uniform of a Crucible Industries general floor worker — not the specialized smelter or weld crew kits, but the backbone ops staff who keep materials moving, machinery logged, and shift quotas met. The jacket is a flame-resistant charcoal canvas work coat, thigh-length, with snap-off sleeves for hot-floor adaptability. The Crucible hex-and-anvil logo is heat-transfer printed across the upper back in dull orange. Chest pockets on both sides, one with a clear-window ID slot. Beneath it, a crew-neck work shirt in faded safety orange — washed to a muted clay tone after dozens of industrial cycles — with reinforced elbow patches in matching canvas. The shirt has a left-sleeve channel running from shoulder to wrist: an aug-accommodation track stitched into the seam to allow chrome arm hardware to sit flush without bunching fabric. Work trousers are heavy-gauge charcoal canvas with hammer loops, a full ring of tool eyelets at the waist, and double-stitched thighs. Boots are thick-soled composite safety boots with a puncture-resistant midsole and a self-tightening ankle strap. Safety goggles on an elastic band hang around the neck when not in use — scratched lenses, one replacement arm in a different color. A hardshell bump cap in safety orange sits low on the brow, often pushed back off the forehead by mid-shift.

Crucible Smelter Operations Thermal Suit#

Workers operating in Crucible's active smelting floors and high-temperature fabrication cells wear this suit as their primary layer of protection between themselves and environments that can reach 900 degrees Celsius at the point of operation. The outer shell is a ceramic-fiber composite woven over a reflective aluminized barrier — stiff at the shoulders and chest where heat exposure is greatest, more flexible at the joints where mobility is necessary for crane controls and pour-gate operations. Crucible's safety division mandates this suit for all smelter floor personnel regardless of augmentation status, which creates ongoing friction with workers whose chrome runs hot and requires additional ventilation. The suit incorporates mesh ventilation channels along the flanks that help but don't fully resolve the conflict.

The suit is orange-red — Crucible's floor safety color — with black trim and a reflective stripe across the back and both arms. The Crucible wordmark is heat-stamped on the left chest. It weighs approximately 4.2 kilograms fully assembled, and workers on eight-hour smelter shifts describe the weight as the defining physical fact of their working day. Tail accommodations exist: a sealed rear port with a fire-rated closure flap rated to the same thermal standard as the rest of the suit. Workers with significant geneware modifications that increase surface area — fur, scales, dermal ridges — report significantly elevated heat stress and have been the subject of three ongoing Crucible labor grievances regarding suit design inadequacy.

Crucible Weld & Fab Supervisory Jacket#

Crucible's floor supervisors wear this jacket as a mark of rank that separates them from the standard-issue maintenance jumpsuits of the line workers below them. Constructed from a flame-resistant aramid-cotton blend with a reflective Crucible anvil logo across the back in heat-resistant silver ink, the jacket is rated for incidental weld splash and short-duration heat exposure up to 400°C. Color is Crucible's signature industrial orange over a graphite underlayer.

The jacket is built wide at the shoulders to fit the range of body types that come up through Crucible's apprenticeship tracks, including workers with significant upper-body chrome — reinforced seams at the shoulder accommodate most cybernetic arm attachment points, and the back panel is cut to allow tail-loop access for geneware-modified supervisors. It's not glamorous work wear, but it's built to last: most supervisors wear the same jacket for 5–8 years before it needs replacement, and the culture around Crucible sites means a battered jacket is a sign of experience, not neglect.

Dawngate Lacquered Silk Blouse#

Dawngate is a Tier 5 atelier operating from a single floor of the Spire's commercial level, appointment-only, with a six-week lead time on bespoke pieces. Their lacquered silk blouse is a ready-to-wear offering — which at Dawngate means a limited run of forty per season, hand-finished. The silk is a cultivated Chinese-heritage strain crossed with a lab-grown fiber that gives the weave a particular drape: heavier than standard silk, with a subtle structured memory that holds a fold without stiffening. The 'lacquer' refers to the finishing process — a thin botanical resin application that gives the fabric a deep, almost wet-looking sheen in dark jewel tones. Midnight blue, deep amber, a near-black with burgundy undertones.

The collar is a wide mandarin-to-open-neck hybrid, and the cuffs are single-button with a hidden pleat that allows full wrist range of motion. There are no visible seams on the exterior — all construction is internal, with French seams throughout. Wearing it, you are aware of the weight and the sound it makes when you move. That awareness is intentional.

Dockside Cold-Chain Handler's Day Rig#

Built for the refrigerated cargo holds and cold-chain loading bays of Meridian Harbor's bulk freight terminals, this layered kit prioritizes thermal retention without sacrificing the freedom of movement needed to work a full shift. The outermost layer is a high-collar insulated vest in safety orange with black ripstop side panels, harbor authority reflective striping at the shoulders, and a large patch pocket on the chest marked with the worker's dock assignment number in hand-written marker. Beneath the vest sits a heavyweight fleece-lined work shirt in deep navy, quarter-zip with a reinforced collar that folds high against wind off the lake. The shirt has a left-sleeve BCI port pass-through — a simple rubberized grommet that lets wrist-mounted interface hardware route cleanly without bunching fabric. Trousers are insulated canvas in charcoal with wide-set cargo pockets, boot-cut leg opening to clear ankle-height footwear, and neoprene knee pads sewn in permanently. Boots are waterproof pull-on dock boots with a steel toe, non-slip tread rated for wet deck surfaces, and a calf-height shaft. A thermal balaclava in navy rolls down to a neck gaiter when the bay doors are open.

Dockside Cold-Store Handler's Layered Full Kit#

Workers managing cold-storage freight at Meridian Harbor's interior docking bays — pulling cryogenic cargo containers, operating pallet movers in sub-zero holds, stacking refrigerated units — dress for the cold first and everything else second. The base is a full-body thermal underlayer in pale grey moisture-wicking synth-fleece, close-fitting with flat seams to prevent pressure points under the outer gear, and a reinforced collar that can be pulled up over the lower face. Over this goes an insulated bib-overall in burnt orange — the standard color for cold-store certified workers — made from a quilted synth-nylon shell with hollow-fiber fill, rated to minus twenty Celsius. The bib straps are wide and padded, adjustable with quick-release buckles, and the side panels have stretch inserts for movement. A matching insulated work jacket in the same burnt orange goes over the bibs, with a sherpa-lined collar that folds up into a partial hood, heavy-duty glove loops on the cuffs, and a left-chest panel embroidered with the worker's facility number and a cold-store certification badge in reflective thread. Gauntlet-style insulated work gloves in black synth-leather with grip-dot palms hang from the cuff loops when not in use. The boots are wide-last insulated waterproof work boots with a composite safety toe, rated for cold-store floors, with oil and slip resistant soles. A thermal balaclava in grey synth-fleece covers the head and neck, leaving only the eyes clear, over which workers often clip a polycarbonate face shield on a bump cap.

Drift Collective Salvage-Bead Necklace#

A necklace strung with beads made from salvaged materials — circuit board fragments, polished machine screws, flattened bullet casings, tumbled glass from broken displays. Each bead represents something the wearer found, survived, or chose to remember. No two necklaces are the same.

In Shelf communities where the Drift Collective's aesthetic holds influence, the Salvage-Bead Necklace functions as a wearable autobiography. People who know the code can read the beads like a timeline — this one is from the factory collapse, this one is from the year the water went bad, this one is a casing from the night everything changed.

Drift Market Vendor's Layered Stand#

The drift markets of the Shelf run in all weather — acid drizzle, heat inversions, the particular cold that comes off the lake when the wind pushes through the corridor. This outfit is engineered for standing still in all of it, which is a different survival problem than moving through it. The base is a wide-collared tunic in deep rust, the fabric a dense cotton-synthetic weave that has faded unevenly from washing in reclaimed water, leaving a mottled pattern that looks almost intentional — warmer rust at the center, washed-out ochre at the hems and cuffs. Over it, a vest in dark gray felted material, the felt dense enough to be nearly rigid, carries twelve external pockets of varying sizes across its front and interior: this is a vendor's vest, and each pocket holds something specific. The left breast pocket has a slit for a tablet-thin transaction reader, the edges of the slit worn smooth from a thousand insertions. Layered over the vest is a wide-bodied over-shirt in faded olive waxed canvas, left unbuttoned and worn as a light jacket, its wrists rolled and secured with loops of self-repair tape. Trousers are wide-cut in dark charcoal, the fabric thick and slightly stiff, with two deep front pockets and a broad waistband that sits high — practical for standing. At the hem, the trousers are folded once and secured with small clips, a Shelf tailoring solution for fabric bought long and not cut. Shoes are flat and broad, slip-on style in cracked dark rubber, the soles thick and slightly worn to the outer edge from standing on uneven market-ground. A long scarf in faded burgundy and gray plaid — synthetic wool, clearly machine-woven but worn soft — is wrapped twice around the neck and tucked into the vest, one end left to fall loose. Around the waist, a broad apron in heavy stained canvas covers the lower front of the outfit; its pockets are full and its surface is stained with the evidence of a dozen different trades.

Driftclean Pressed Occasion Dress — Shelf Cut#

A knee-length dress in a deep navy synth-polyester that photographs darker than it looks in person, which is a feature the vendor actively advertises. The fabric is thin enough to fold into a pocket-sized square, which matters when storage space is limited. The cut is universally generous — a single size-adjustable drawstring at the waist allows it to fit a wide range of bodies, including those with minor geneware modifications. A small tail accommodation slit has been roughly cut into the back seam on some units and left raw-edged, a field modification that has become so common the vendor now includes it as an option at point of sale.

This dress exists because people on the Shelf have occasions too. It is sold in market stalls alongside cleaning supplies and ration supplements, and it is priced to be reachable on a single shift's pay. The fabric pills after three washes but holds its color. It is not beautiful in any technical sense. It is appropriate, and on the Shelf, appropriate is enough.

A two-piece suit assembled from mismatched but color-matched salvage: jacket from one donor garment, trousers from another. The Driftclean Collective operates out of a Tier 1 basement laundry, doing alterations and suit-matching for people who need to look legitimate for legal proceedings, employment interviews, or family events. The jacket is taken in with interior basting stitches that hold but won't survive aggressive movement. Driftclean Shelf Best Dress Coat#

A knee-length dress coat that has passed through at least three owners, its original color somewhere between charcoal and rust depending on the light. The lining has been replaced once with mismatched poly-satin, and the lapels are hand-pressed with a hot pipe rather than an iron. The buttons don't match but they're all accounted for. No augment ports, no smart fabric, no climate regulation. What it offers is dignity on a budget measured in single-digit Quanta. Neither is the careful, nearly invisible mending at the right shoulder seam. Both are noticed by everyone in the room, and no one says anything.

Driftmarket Vendor's Layered Street Kit#

The working uniform of a Circuit street food vendor or open-air market stall operator — not corponation-issued, but assembled with the same utilitarian logic, built from pieces sourced across market stalls and discount Circuit outlets. The base is a long-sleeved henley in deep rust-orange, a color that reads as warm and approachable against the grey of Circuit streets and incidentally hides most food stains. Over it goes a heavy canvas apron in waxed dark olive, full bib-style with wide front pockets — one pocket holds a flat-folded order tablet, the other a collection of stylus pens, zip ties, and a folded cloth for wiping surfaces. The apron strings are doubled and cross-wrapped at the back rather than tying at the waist, distributing weight better for someone who stands for ten hours straight. Around the hips, a nylon utility belt carries a compact heat-seal tool for packaging, a change pouch in worn black leather, and a folded thermal bag sleeve for keeping items at temperature.

Trousers are straight-cut black synth-canvas with a slight stretch through the thigh, comfortable for standing and bending, with reinforced pockets. On the feet: a low-cut black rubber-soled work shoe with a wide toe box and a textured grip sole rated for wet and greasy surfaces — the kind of shoe that goes unremarked until someone tries to work without them. A short-brimmed cap in the same rust-orange as the henley keeps overhead rig lights and rain off the face; a name or stall identifier is often written in white paint marker on the front brim. Hands are bare — the vendor's hands are their instrument — but a pair of thin heat-resistant gloves is folded into the apron pocket for grill work. The whole kit is civilian, personal, and carries the smell of whatever they're selling.

Driftpile Acidwalk Full Kit#

Built around a rubberized poncho-coat in matte black that has long since faded to an uneven charcoal, this outfit is a Shelf rain-walker's solution to the Great Lakes acid season. Dunbar & Seo Longcoat#

Dunbar & Seo is old money in the Meridian 88 tailoring world — a label that has been producing bespoke and ready-to-wear at the high end of the market for four decades, long enough to have dressed three generations of Tier 4 and Tier 5 families. The Longcoat is their statement outerwear piece: a floor-length structured coat in a cashmere-wool blend that is available in six house colors and can be ordered in any color with sufficient lead time. The silhouette is severe and intentional — high collar, clean front placket with concealed closures, minimal surface detail, and a cut that falls straight from shoulder to hem with an almost architectural rigidity. It is the coat of a person who has decided that their outerwear does not need to explain itself. Tier 5 clients order these in volume; Tier 4 clients save for one and wear it for a decade. The ready-to-wear line starts at Φ1,200; fully bespoke begins at Φ4,000 and climbs from there.

Durovex Sentinel Armored Jacket#

From the outside, the Sentinel looks like a well-made moto jacket — slightly structured, medium-weight, available in black or dark olive with minimal hardware. Durovex is a Tier 3 to 4 personal protection brand that sells legally with appropriate licensing, though the Sentinel is popular enough that unlicensed versions circulate in the Tier 2 markets. Duskiron Elder's Long Coat Set#

Some Shelf residents have been there long enough to accumulate something more than survival gear — they've accumulated presence. This outfit belongs to that category. The centerpiece is a floor-length duster coat in deep charcoal wool, its original weave still visible beneath decades of weathering, patching, and treatment. The coat has been re-lined three times — the current lining is a patchwork of mylar emergency blanket sections sewn between layers of salvaged fleece, creating a thermal barrier that crinkles faintly when the wearer moves. The hem has been re-cut and rehemmed four times as it frayed, each cut visible as a lighter band across the lower third. Patch repairs across the back and shoulders are applied in a deliberate overlapping scale pattern, using scraps of brown leather, black rubber sheeting, and gray synthetic canvas — not haphazard but arranged, almost decorative. Beneath the coat is a high-neck tunic in faded rust linen — a style that borrows from Chinese changshan proportions but cut shorter, the mandarin collar reinforced with salvaged leather trim. Trousers are heavy dark wool, wide-legged and cuffed, worn over thick knit gaiters that tuck into wide-toe boots resoled so many times the sole is now thicker than the original. The boots are wrapped at the ankle in strips of black rubber tape for waterproofing. On the hands, fingerless gloves in cracked brown leather — the fingers cut away cleanly, the edges sealed with black rubber cement. A wide-brimmed hat in waxed canvas, stained gray and rust, completes the silhouette. This person has survived long enough to have a look.

Duskrow Moto Jacket#

A motorcycle jacket built for the Shelf and lower Tier 2, where looking hard is sometimes the only armor you've got. The Duskrow is made from bonded synth-hide — not leather, not pretending to be — in a flat, worn-in black with faint horizontal ribbing across the shoulders and forearms. The cut is boxy enough to move in, with an asymmetric zip closure, two chest pockets with snap flaps, and a wide lapel collar that can be turned up against the wind off the lake. Pre-scuffed at the elbows. That's not a flaw. That's the design.

People who wear the Duskrow aren't trying to impress anyone at a Tier 3 wine bar. They're couriers, fixers, gig workers who ride secondhand mopeds through the Shelf's cracked-asphalt corridors. The jacket shows up in markets, in dive bars, in the back of dispatch vans. It holds its shape after a fall. It doesn't crack in the cold. It's the kind of jacket you hand down.

Dustveil Patchwork Ghost Operative Set#

At first glance this is a Tier 1 survivor's layered coat — mismatched panels of deep olive, charcoal, and faded indigo stitched together in a pattern that reads as poverty-mended patchwork. The footwear is deliberate contrast: battered high-top boots with mismatched lace colors, a classic Shelf aesthetic that completes the poverty read while concealing a hardened composite sole and a toe-cap rated for door-breach kicks. A wide-brim hat in sun-faded olive with a low crown completes the silhouette, obscuring facial geometry from overhead surveillance drones.

Fenrir Thermal-Arc Parka#

A mid-length parka designed for Meridian 88's brutal lake winters, manufactured by Fenrir — a Scandinavian-heritage brand that opened a Great Lakes production facility in 2171. The outer shell is a tightly woven ripstop nylon in matte black, navy, or a deep forest green. The interior uses a graphene-filament heating mesh powered by a thin flexible battery pack sewn into the left side panel — a USB-C style connector at the hem lets you charge from any standard port. Ferrogrip Pressline Assembly Day Rig#

The standard daily rig for pressline assembly workers at mid-tier fabrication facilities — not corponation-issued but purchased through the factory commissary and worn by thousands of floor workers across Circuit. The coverall is the centerpiece: a single-piece garment in deep industrial charcoal, made from Ferrogrip's proprietary ToughWeave synth-canvas that resists minor spark burns, hydraulic fluid, and metal shavings. It runs from ankle to collar, fitted through the torso with a gusseted crotch for crouching and a back pleat for reach. The chest has two utility pockets with press-stud closures, and the right shoulder carries a loop-and-clip strip for hanging safety glasses or a face shield. A removable hi-vis orange safety vest goes over the top — mesh-backed for ventilation, with reflective yellow-green chevrons front and rear and a name patch strip in white across the chest, typically filled with a hand-written or heat-stamped first name. Beneath the coverall, workers wear a moisture-wicking short-sleeve compression undershirt in grey, often customized with personal markings or a faded band tee worn underneath for morale. Heavy steel-toe boots in matte black with a reinforced ankle cuff and oil-resistant sole complete the lower half. A welding-grade fabric cap — flat brim, charcoal, with a rear port cutout stitched open for neural plug access — sits on the head, often backwards.

Ferroink Chromepulse Circuit Dancer Set#

Ferroink Signal-Break Operative Set#

This set leads with a structured moto-cut jacket in deep navy-black with an ink-wash ferrous brown panel running diagonally across the left chest and right shoulder — a deliberate asymmetry that makes the jacket memorable without being flashy. Beneath the jacket, a mandarin-collar shirt in dark teal shot-silk synthetic provides a layer of respectability — this outfit passes at a Tier 3 establishment without triggering dress-code scrutiny. Footwear is a polished synthetic leather chelsea boot in dark brown, square-toe, with a reinforced steel toe cap concealed under the finish. A low-profile comm earpiece clips behind the ear with a near-invisible matte-black wire running under the collar.

Floodwall Grandmother's Walking Coat#

At first glance this looks like nothing — a long, shapeless coat in faded black over dark gray trousers and flat boots. Then you get closer and realize you're looking at a masterwork of Shelf textile engineering, assembled over decades. The coat is floor-length, originally a double-breasted wool-blend overcoat that has been so comprehensively rebuilt it retains only its silhouette. The body is now a patchwork of at least eleven distinct fabric sources — sections of military rain shell, cut-up transit worker hi-vis (the orange faded to a pale gold), thermal underlayer fleece, waxed cotton scraps, and what looks like the back panel of a corporate uniform jacket with the logo still faintly visible beneath two seasons of grime. The patches are stitched with extraordinary precision, tight cross-hatching along every seam, and the overall effect is a coat that looks like a map. The collar is wide and can be turned up to cover the lower half of the face; the inside is lined with strips of reflective emergency blanket sewn in a herringbone pattern. Trousers are straight-cut dark charcoal, heavy cotton-synthetic blend, with a single deep side pocket on each leg and a drawstring at the ankle — Shelf standard for keeping vermin and water out. Underneath is a turtleneck in faded rust-brown, the neck worn smooth from years of contact. Boots are flat, wide-lasted, resoled in thick black rubber with a slight platform from the accumulated layers; the uppers are scuffed to a near-suede finish. The only accessories are a hand-knotted scarf in dark olive and gray — clearly hand-spun from salvaged fiber — worn loose enough to pull up, and a canvas bag on a thick shoulder strap, its exterior covered in small embroidered symbols in thread colors that don't match anything else in the outfit.

Graymark Thermal Shell#

Graymark sits in a specific niche: thermal regulation technology at a price point that Tier 3 buyers can justify as a long-term investment. The Thermal Shell is a mid-length jacket — not quite a parka, not quite a shell — with an embedded heating element network powered by a thin-film battery panel integrated into the back lining. The exterior is a matte-finish nylon in a medium gray that photographs as almost any color depending on light conditions. The jacket is cut slim enough to look intentional in a Tier 3 office context and practical enough to actually use on the lakefront. Battery life is approximately eight hours on medium setting.

Light, fast, and visually complex in a way that reads as intentional from a distance but dissolves into improvisation up close. Gene-mod accommodation is evident: the lower back of the trousers has a soft tail-loop stitched in — currently unused but present, suggesting the wearer either has a tail mod or is planning for one. Greymarrow Detach-Panel Night Ops Set#

Everything about this set is designed to change. The primary jacket is a hip-length blouson in matte grey-brown — the color of unpainted ferrocrete, utterly unremarkable — with four snap-off exterior panels: two chest, two shoulder. Each panel swaps out independently, and a runner carrying a small pouch of alternates can change the jacket's visible silhouette and color blocking in under ninety seconds. The base jacket beneath the panels is plain enough to wear alone. Inside, a double-wall front panel conceals a rigid holster frame that can be reconfigured for two compacts, one full-frame, or a row of tool loops. The back yoke has a full spinal channel — a wide open-seam corridor running from collar to hem that accommodates external spinal rig hardware, closing around it with a series of silent magnetic tabs. Gene-compatible rear venting panels accommodate non-functional wings or large dorsal geneware modifications with snap-bar expansion. Paired trousers are in near-black slate with a maroon pinstripe too subtle to read at distance — Tier 2 enough to vanish in a crowd, Tier 3 enough to enter a building lobby. Thigh zip pockets are scanner-lined to mask small metal objects from passive detection. Footwear is a flat-soled runner's shoe in dark graphite synthetic mesh over a hard composite plate, lace-free with a single diagonal strap closure. A thin balaclava in matching grey-brown microfibre is folded in the inside collar pocket — full face cover in two seconds, gone in three.

GridFeed Street Cart Vendor All-Weather Stand Rig#

The working uniform of someone who runs a food cart at a Circuit-level transit hub or factory gate, assembled for maximum function across a twelve-hour outdoor shift in Meridian's unpredictable acid-rain cycles. The outermost layer is a full-length rubberized apron in deep charcoal with a GridFeed street-brand logo — a stylized fork wrapped in a signal wave — stamped in white across the chest bib. It's not a corponation; GridFeed is a small Circuit-level vendor supply cooperative that sells aprons, cart equipment, and bulk food inputs to independent vendors, and the logo on the apron is a mark of membership, not employment. Beneath the apron is a long-sleeve thermal work shirt in burnt orange with ribbed cuffs, a relaxed collar, and two breast pockets; the left pocket holds a small order stylus and a folded cloth for wiping down surfaces. Trousers are dark navy cargo-cut in a stain-resistant synth-cotton blend, with a wide waistband and a deep front pocket configured to carry a card reader and a personal comm unit simultaneously.

Footwear is the Ashgrove Linework Work Boot in black with a non-slip sole rated for wet and grease-slicked surfaces — essential for anyone working around hot oil and condensation runoff. The head is covered with a tall white cook's cap or, in rain, a waterproof brimmed hat in matching charcoal with the GridFeed logo repeated on the front. Hands cycle between bare (for fine work) and nitrile gloves (for food handling), kept in a side apron pocket in a continuous rotation. The gene-compatible cut of the apron includes a reinforced tail slot at the back lower hem — a wide, finished opening that accommodates a full prehensile tail without bunching or restriction, since enough Circuit-level vendors have geneware modifications that GridFeed built it into their standard apron pattern. The whole rig smells permanently of whatever's on the menu today: chili oil, fermented soy, spiced protein paste, rain-steam.

Gridline Street Vendor's Weather Layering Set#

A practical, self-curated layering kit worn by Circuit-level street food vendors, market stall operators, and mobile cart workers who spend full shifts exposed to M88's variable weather — acid-rain squalls, thermal inversions, and the cold lake-corridor wind that scours the elevated walkways. The outermost layer is a waist-length anorak in weatherproof sage-green synth-wax, hood cinched with a toggle drawstring, chest pocket sealed with a magnetic flap. A small embroidered patch on the left shoulder reads the vendor's licensed stall number in Circuit's market registry — required by city ordinance, often accompanied by a handmade decorative border the vendor has added themselves. Beneath the anorak, a heavy-duty apron in charcoal canvas covers the torso from collar to knee, cross-back straps distributing the weight of deep front pockets loaded with tools, condiment packets, a card reader, and small wares. The apron's bib has a transparent ID-sleeve pocket for the vendor's Circuit commerce license. Under the apron, a rust-orange thermal mid-layer pullover with a funnel neck provides insulation. Trousers are dark olive cargo-cut synth-twill, knee-reinforced for the crouching and kneeling of restocking and equipment maintenance. Footwear is a pair of Ashgrove Linework Work Boots — oil-resistant flat sole, composite toe, ankle-height.

This isn't a uniform — it's an ecosystem of practical choices refined over seasons. Vendors working gene-compatible builds often have their apron straps widened or the anorak hood enlarged to accommodate horns or enhanced ear structures; most of these modifications are hand-sewn. The stall number patch is the only branding required, but vendors frequently add layers of personal expression: painted apron pockets, lucky charms clipped to the anorak zipper pull, an ancestor's recipe card laminated and tucked behind the ID sleeve.

GridPatch Night Maintenance Street-to-Site Rig#

Infrastructure maintenance workers who pull night shifts on Circuit's open-air conduit grid — fixing cracked pipes, patching acid-rain erosion on overpass supports, splicing power lines at two in the morning — wear a rig that has to take them from the transit stop to the job site and back without standing out as a target. The outer shell is a hooded work jacket in slate grey synth-canvas, mid-thigh length with a drawstring hem, raglan sleeves cut wide enough to accommodate a full chrome arm prosthetic with room for a tool strap underneath. Subtle reflective piping runs along the hood edge and cuffs — visible to vehicles but not obvious from a distance. The jacket back carries a large embroidered patch: the GridPatch municipal maintenance logo, a stylized circuit-board hexagon in faded yellow-orange on grey. Underneath is a heavyweight navy henley in thermal synth-cotton, long-sleeved with reinforced elbow patches in darker navy canvas. The trousers are Fenmark ToughSeam-style in charcoal, with articulated knees, a waterproof coating on the lower legs and seat, and six pockets including two large cargo pockets on the thigh sealed with hook-and-bar closures. A tool belt in worn black leather-analog sits over the waistband — spanner loops, a multi-tool holster, and a small lamp clip. Boots are mid-cut waterproof work boots with a composite toe and deep lug sole for wet grating and scaffold work. A knit neck gaiter in charcoal doubles as a face cover in acid-drizzle conditions, and a battered hard-foam bump cap with a built-in LED strip completes the head.

Groundswell // Drowned City Tour Tee#

Black short-sleeve tee in a slightly heavier-than-average cotton-synth blend, with a screen-printed design on the chest: a stylized skyline half-submerged in abstract water, rendered in white and electric teal. The tour tee has become something of a marker in certain circles — people who were actually at the shows wear them differently than people who bought them after. Both groups exist, and both are legitimate.

Haelan ClimateCore Long-Sleeve Shirt#

A long-sleeve button-down that regulates its own thermal output through a distributed micro-filament network woven into the fabric. The shirt reads ambient temperature and the wearer's skin temperature simultaneously, adjusting the filament activation to maintain a preset comfort band. The result is that you can wear this in a cold transit tunnel and a heated office and feel roughly the same in both. The fabric looks and feels like a standard fine-weave synth-linen — matte, professional, available in eight colors including a sharp teal called 'Caspian' and a warm grey called 'Mineral.'

Haelan markets this as their 'executive productivity' line — the idea being that you think better when you're not adjusting your thermostat every twenty minutes. The shirt pairs a legitimate tech feature with clean, conservative styling that reads as professional in any Tier 3 or 4 setting. The collar stays crisp. The cuffs have a single button.

Halcyon Athletics Riverton Varsity#

A classic varsity jacket — wool body in team colors, leather sleeves, ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Halcyon Athletics produces these in bulk for the city's recreational and semi-professional sports leagues, but the Riverton model is their retail line: the same silhouette, same construction, but sold in generic colorways and without league insignia so anyone can wear one. Available in combinations of navy-cream, crimson-grey, and black-gold. A chenille 'H' patch is sewn on the left chest. The snap-front closure is solid and the pockets are generous.

Varsity jackets never fully went away, and in Meridian 88 they've had a sustained revival as casual wear across Tier 2 and Tier 3. The Riverton sits at a price point where it's aspirational for the Shelf and accessible for working-class buyers. It's the jacket of high school athletes who aged out, of people who wanted to belong to something and found this a reasonable substitute, and of anyone who just thinks the silhouette looks good — which it does.

Halcyon Variform Lace Boot#

A clean, utilitarian ankle boot with a modular toe box that expands or contracts via a small dial recessed into the heel. Halo Dynamics Softshell BCI Pullover#

Halo Dynamics makes hardware and, increasingly, the clothing designed to interface with it. The Softshell BCI Pullover is a crew-neck pullover in a matte charcoal softshell fabric that looks, at a glance, like a normal athletic top. Look closer and you'll see the subtle port-access panels at the base of the skull — two small magnetic flap covers, flush with the fabric, that allow BCI maintenance and hardware access without removing the garment. The fabric itself has a low-conductivity inner lining that reduces interference with surface-mounted BCI hardware. It's not glamorous tech, but it's practical.

The cut is clean and slightly athletic. It works as a standalone top or an underlayer. Halo Dynamics includes it in the standard 'adaptation kit' sold alongside their mid-range BCI implants, which means a significant percentage of Tier 3 BCI users own one. It reads as tech-adjacent without screaming it — someone wearing this is probably augmented, but not necessarily heavily.

Halversen & Co. Handknit Wool-Analog Sweater#

Halversen & Co. occupies a strange position in Meridian 88's fashion ecosystem: a Tier 5 label that sells hand-finished knitwear that looks, at first glance, like something a grandmother made. The sweaters are produced by a cooperative of master knitters working in small batches — each piece has visible evidence of human hands in the work, slight irregularities in the tension that machine production can't replicate. The wool-analog fiber is exceptionally fine, derived from a bioengineered fiber that mimics the warmth and softness of Shetland wool without any of its variability. This particular model is a boxy, slightly oversized crew-neck in a natural undyed cream, with a textured cable-knit front panel and ribbed sleeves.

The people who buy Halversen & Co. are not showing off — or rather, they're showing off in a way that only other people who know will understand. The sweater costs more than most Tier 2 workers earn in a month. It looks like something you could find at a secondhand market. That tension is entirely deliberate.

Hearthpatch Elder's Walking Coat Set#

Not every Shelf outfit is built for running or hiding. This one is built for endurance, dignity, and the long walk. The centerpiece is a full-length coat — originally a women's overcoat in deep burgundy wool, now faded to a dusty maroon with a gray undertone — that has been repaired so many times it has become a new garment. Every patch is a different fabric: a square of dark green canvas at the left elbow, a strip of black synthrubber at the hem where puddle-rot set in, a careful re-weaving of the right lapel with rust-colored thread that doesn't quite match but holds the shape. The coat falls to mid-calf and is belted with a wide leather strap, worn and darkened with age, the original buckle replaced with a hand-bent wire clasp. Beneath it, a layered situation: a thick ribbed turtleneck in off-white that's been washed gray, tucked into wide-leg trousers in dark brown heavy cotton, the waistband reinforced with a second strip of fabric sewn over the original. Shoes are flat, wide-last, in cracked dark leather resoled twice in thick rubber — the kind of shoe built for someone who stands and walks all day and needs their feet to still work at the end of it. A wide wool headwrap in faded teal and rust, gene-compatible in its generous size and soft drape, covers the head and wraps loosely at the neck. Hands are bare. The coat's interior has been fitted with four hand-sewn pockets, deep and flat, invisible from outside.

Helios-Nomad Stormline Shell#

A minimalist hardshell rain jacket from Helios-Nomad, a mid-tier outdoor brand that pivoted hard into urban commuter wear in the 2180s. The shell is a three-layer bonded membrane — waterproof, windproof, breathable — in a clean matte finish. No visible seams on the outside; all taped internally. The cut is slim without being restrictive. Hood stows flat into the collar. Two hand pockets and a chest pocket, all waterproof-zip. Available in a range of solid colors: slate, sand, a particular deep teal that's become associated with the brand.

This is the jacket you wear in Meridian 88's persistent lake-effect weather — the cold drizzle that runs October through April, the sudden squalls off Lake Michigan that soak you in ninety seconds. It's practical and it looks it. Tier 2 commuters wear it because it works. Tier 3 buyers wear it because it also happens to look clean. It photographs well. It layers over everything. It's the closest thing to a universal jacket the city has.

Helix Corp Compliance Tier Pressed Day Set#

The quintessential Tier 3 corporate uniform, issued with minor variations across a dozen corponation subsidiaries. A collarless button-front shirt in Helix Corp's proprietary 'administratum weave' — a mid-weight polysynth blend in muted slate-blue that resists wrinkling and absorbs approximately forty percent of ambient sweat. Straight-leg trousers in matching slate-grey with a permanent crease ironed in at the factory, worn smooth at the inner thigh from daily transit seating. A lanyard with a printed-polymer ID badge completes the look — the badge worn front-facing at chest height as policy dictates.

The shoes show buffing marks where scuffs have been polished out repeatedly. This is a person who has worn this outfit, or one exactly like it, every working day for years.

Holloway & Drax Culinary Line Uniform Set#

Holloway & Drax supplies kitchen uniforms to the majority of Meridian 88's mid-tier restaurant operations, hotel kitchens, and corporate cafeteria contracts. Their standard culinary line set includes a double-breasted chef's coat, high-waist utility trousers, and an apron — all in white with the subtle H&D chain-link logo printed at the collar. The coat fabric is a treated cotton-synthfiber blend rated for sustained heat exposure up to 200°C surface contact, with reinforced forearm panels where hot pan contact is most common. Buttons are magnetic-closure rather than traditional — faster to remove in case of spill burns, and replaceable without tools.

The set is designed with practical geneware accommodation throughout. The coat includes a rear vent panel with a hook-and-eye closure for tail clearance, and the headwear component — a structured cap rather than a traditional toque — is available in three sizes with horn-clearance cutouts on the crown, sealed with food-safe silicone edging to maintain hygienic standards. Workers with ear geneware (pointed, extended, or mobile) can substitute the cap for a certified hair-containment band at supervisor discretion. Augment compatibility is addressed through reinforced elbow patches that sit clear of standard forearm port housings. The set is washable at industrial temperatures and rated for 200 cycles before replacement is recommended — in practice, most line cooks push well past that.

Holstrom Lakefront Parka#

A serious working parka designed for the brutal winter winds that come screaming off Lake Michigan through the Shelf and lower Tier 2 corridors. Cut long to the mid-thigh, it features a quilted recycled-fiber shell in faded olive or slate gray, with a massive hood that cinches down to a face-width opening via toggle cord. Shelf residents layer these over everything in winter. Couriers swear by them. You see them at bus stops, at processing plant gates, at Tier 2 market stalls — functional, honest, slightly shapeless.

Hookline Independent Dock & Haul Street Kit#

Not company-issued — this is the working kit of an independent dock laborer, day-hire cargo handler, or gig-economy freight mover who doesn't work for any single corponation long enough to get a uniform. It's assembled from a mix of quality street-label and surplus, and it holds together through deliberate choice rather than institutional supply. The outer layer is a surplus-style work jacket in faded navy waxed cotton, hood stuffed into the collar, with chest pockets reinforced by street-sewn bar tacks. Across the left sleeve, someone has stenciled a small orange triangle with a number — a dock lot designation, or a crew mark, or a union section ID. The jacket's back panel has been slit along the spine and re-laced with industrial paracord to create a crude but effective spinal-rig accommodation channel. Underneath is a heavyweight charcoal henley with three-button placket, thick enough to function as a mid-layer without a separate underlayer. Trousers are navy canvas work pants cut wide in the thigh for movement, with external knee pad channels (pads currently in), cargo pockets on both legs, and a reinforced seat. A wide webbing belt with a heavy D-ring carries a hook tool, a clip for a work lamp, and a battered multi-use utility holster. Boots are thick-soled dock walkers with steel toe and side-zip entry, scuffed to grey at the toe caps. A knit balaclava worn pulled back as a thick watch cap covers the head, grey with a single faded orange stripe.

Hookline Independent Freight Night Haul Kit#

The working uniform of an independent dock and freight hauler running night shifts on the Circuit-level cargo corridors — no corponation logo, no issued kit, everything sourced personally and maintained obsessively. The base is a heavyweight dark navy cargo trouser from Goretek — HaulMaster cut, with reinforced inner thighs, six pockets including two deep side-cargo pockets with compression buckles, and a wide belt loop arrangement that accommodates a tool-and-tether harness. The trouser legs are slightly flared at the ankle to accommodate a digitigrade leg prosthetic on the left side, the seam there hand-opened and restitched with orange industrial thread — a visible repair that's also a practical modification. On top: a Sable Freight thermal henley in dark brown, long-sleeved, with a kangaroo chest pocket that holds a flex-screen work manifest. Over it, a high-vis orange safety vest — generic market-bought, no branding — with reflective silver strips at chest and hem, multiple D-ring attachment points, and a built-in radio holster on the left chest.

Boots are Dockmaster Deepwade — waterproof, steel-toe, ankle-height with a side-zip for fast removal. A wide-brimmed matte-black rain hat with a synth-wax finish and a hi-vis orange band around the crown keeps acid-drizzle off the neck. Thick fingerless work gloves in gray synth-leather leave the fingertips free for manifest-screen operation. A battered personal light — magnetic clip-mount, warm amber beam — clips to the vest's shoulder strap. The whole kit is dark, functional, and anonymous: no name patch, no affiliation. Just the work.
