Hookline Independent Nightside Dock Kit#

Not a corponation uniform — this is what an independent dock hauler puts together from reliable street brands and surplus, built for the night shift at Meridian Harbor's outer berths where the light is bad and the cargo manifests are sometimes deliberately vague. The foundation is a heavyweight charcoal canvas work shirt from Sable Freight's surplus line, double-stitched at every seam with reinforced pocket flaps on both chest pockets and both forearms. Over it goes a sleeveless hi-vis vest in faded safety orange — originally Meridian Harbor Authority issue, acquired secondhand and thoroughly de-logoed except for a ghost of the original stencil still visible on the back in a slightly different shade of orange. The work trousers are Goretek WorkHold in dark olive, tape-reinforced at the knees and inner thighs, with six pockets including two deep cargo pockets and a slim phone-and-scanner slot along the right hip. A leather tool belt — real leather, Shelf-market sourced and hand-stitched at the buckle — carries a grip wrench, two carabiners, a cargo scanner, and a folded work glove pair.

Bootwise: Dockmaster Deepwade boots in black rubber over a steel shank, laced tight over the trouser cuffs against waterline splash. The head covering is a knit cap in dark charcoal pulled low, or swapped for a hard hat with a cracked brim (the crack is repaired with duct tape in the worker's preferred color — often the only personal color choice in the whole outfit). Hands stay in the work gloves unless actively using the scanner. Aug-compatible at both forearms: the shirt has snap-away forearm panels for chrome arm rigs, a modification the wearer almost certainly did themselves with a seam ripper and a pack of industrial snaps from a Circuit market stall. The whole look says: I know this dock better than anyone, I work for myself, and I don't need your manifest to tell me what's in that container.

Hookline Shelf Patched Crewneck#

Not so much manufactured as assembled. The Hookline Shelf Patched Crewneck starts as a dead-stock athletic crewneck — usually a faded Vance or generic Stride blank — and gets rebuilt by Shelf vendors who layer patches of mismatched fabric across stress points, shoulders, and elbows. Each one is unique. Common patch materials include reclaimed canvas, heavy-gauge denim, printed ad-fabric from torn billboards, and strips of iridescent emergency thermal blanket sewn flat. The stitching is visible, intentional, and loud. Seams are reinforced with waxed thread in contrasting colors.

This is Shelf fashion at its most honest — clothing that acknowledges its own repairs and makes them the design. Kids wear these with defiant pride; adults wear them because it's what they have and it's actually warm. The patches add genuine structural integrity over time. Some have been passed down through two or three hands, accumulating layers until the original garment underneath is more legend than fabric.

Ironclad Concealment Vest#

From the outside, the Ironclad V-series concealment vest looks like a fitted athletic zip-up — a little thicker than a compression shirt, available in black, gray, and a dark olive. The V-series uses a layered construction: an outer shell of abrasion-resistant synthetic, a middle layer of flexible trauma-dispersion paneling (a ceramic-fiber composite that distributes impact without rigid plates), and an inner moisture-wicking layer. It stops low-velocity rounds and disperses blunt trauma. It does not stop high-caliber rifle rounds. The manufacturer is very clear about this in documentation that no one reads.

It's sold through licensed security equipment distributors and, less officially, through several Tier 2 and 3 sporting goods stores that don't ask too many questions. Tier 4 private security staff wear them under dress shirts. Tier 2 neighborhood watch organizers in contested blocks wear them openly. A few Tier 3 journalists who cover the Shelf wear them and don't tell their editors. The vest fits over basic arm augments but requires a custom order for heavy shoulder chrome.

Ironclad Rivet Co. Selvedge Denim Jacket#

A raw selvedge denim jacket in a deep indigo that fades dramatically with wear — the kind of jacket that after two years looks like a topographic map of your life. Ironclad Rivet Co. is a small Tier 2 street brand operating out of a converted print shop in the outer manufacturing belt. They produce maybe eight hundred jackets a year on vintage shuttle looms, and there's usually a wait list. The construction is old-school: bartack stitching at stress points, copper rivets, a blanket-stitch interior seam.

The jacket runs slightly boxy, in keeping with the classic trucker silhouette. It has two chest pockets and two side pockets, all functional. Mechanics, artists, musicians, and anyone who appreciates things built to last wear Ironclad. It's never been advertised. It doesn't need to be.

Ironmarrow ChromeSync Conduit Bodysuit#

A full-torso, long-sleeve bodysuit in matte black with silver-gray routing channels visible as raised seams along the arms, spine, and ribcage. Popular among heavily augmented workers and operatives who need their implants talking to each other.

Ironmarrow Tactical Conceal Vest#

Ironmarrow is a street-level brand with a specific reputation: they make concealment gear that works, priced for people who can't afford Vanthorpe's civilian carry options but need the same function. The Tactical Conceal Vest looks, from the outside, like a plain athletic vest — the kind worn by Tier 2 workers who want an extra layer without a full jacket. Matte black or deep olive, smooth-faced synthetic shell, simple zip front. What the outside doesn't show is the interior: four flat concealment pockets distributed across the torso, reinforced with a light ballistic-grade panel at the chest that provides basic protection against low-velocity impacts. The pockets are sized for a compact sidearm, a blade, documents, or tech.

Ironmarrow sells through three locations in the Midmarket and via a referral-only network in the Shelf. They don't advertise. Their quality control is better than it has any right to be at this price point, which is why people trust them. The vest is worn by fixers, couriers, off-duty security, and anyone who has decided they need to carry something and can't afford to look like they are.

Ironmarrow Work Armor#

Heavy, deliberate, built to take punishment. The centerpiece is a long-sleeved work shirt in dense slate-grey canvas with a mandarin collar, the fabric doubled at the shoulders and elbows with fused patches of scrap ballistic weave — grey-black, slightly shinier than the base cloth, creating a subtle armored texture. Over it goes a full-bib dungaree in dark charcoal, the chest panel reinforced with a sewn-in plate of recovered polycarbonate sheeting — not enough to stop a round but enough to matter in a knife situation or industrial accident. The left bib strap has been replaced with a length of riveted leather, darker and stiffer than the original. Wide-leg construction allows movement and accommodates a right-leg chrome prosthetic: the outer seam of the right leg is left open and fitted with heavy-duty snaps so it can be peeled back for maintenance access without removing the garment. Boots are tall, steel-toed, lace-up in cracked black leather with a composite platform sole — resoled with industrial conveyor belt rubber, grippy and virtually indestructible. A cloth balaclava in faded rust-brown is shoved into a chest pocket. The hands are covered by thick work gloves with the fingertips cut away on three fingers of the right hand for manual dexterity. A wide leather tool belt hangs across the hips, hung with a multi-tool, two carabiners, and a looped length of safety cord.

Ironpass Corridor Maintenance Night Crew Kit#

The working kit of M88's infrastructure maintenance crews — the men, women, and modified persons who descend into the transit corridors, utility conduits, and elevated walkway superstructures during the 0200–0600 dead window when foot traffic drops and repair windows open. The primary garment is a high-visibility coverall in charcoal grey with broad safety-orange shoulder yokes and sleeve stripes, retroreflective tape running the outer leg seams and across the upper back. An Ironpass Infrastructure Services logo — a stylized wrench-and-hex bolt in white — is stenciled on the back panel; a sewn name patch and crew number tag sit on the chest. The coverall has aug-channel seams at both forearms and the upper back, triple-snap closures allowing quick removal of panels for workers with elbow chrome, wrist-mounted tools, or dorsal spinal rigs. Attached to the left thigh is a detachable tool loop panel — a grid of nylon loops and clip rings holding screwdrivers, sealant injectors, wire snips, and a compact diagnostic tablet. A neoprene balaclava in black covers the neck and lower face against tunnel drafts and particulate, with a gap at the crown for BCI port access. The head protection is a low-profile hard hat in safety orange with an integrated LED work light on an articulated arm. Boots are the Ironpass Reinforced Thermal Work Boot — mid-calf, insulated, with a steel midsole against dropped hardware and a chemical-resistant outer sole for corridor solvents.

Night crew kits accumulate personal history fast: sealant stains, scorch marks from conduit work, replacement panels in slightly-off shades of charcoal where the original material wore through. Workers often clip a personal light — a small secondary headlamp or colored chem-glow stick — to their tool panel as a crew identifier in low-visibility conditions. The balaclava's BCI gap is wide enough to accept third-party neural port collars, and several crew members have aftermarket port upgrades that allow direct interface with M88's infrastructure diagnostic network — a technically unauthorized modification that supervisors rely on too heavily to report.

Ironpass Dock & Freight Handler's Full Kit#

A battered but solid head-to-toe kit assembled around the realities of moving heavy cargo on M88's lakefront docks in all weather. The worker wears a yellow hard hat with a cracked brim repaired with silver adhesive tape, a name written in permanent marker on the back: VADUVA-OSEI. Safety glasses hang from the vest's front pocket D-ring. Hands are covered by thick orange leather grip gloves with reinforced palm pads, knuckles worn pale. Boots are heavy lace-up black rubber-over-leather dock boots with a pronounced ankle guard, rated for chemical splash and equipped with a magnetic-latch safety toe. The whole kit smells faintly of hydraulic fluid and lake water. It's functional, unglamorous, and completely honest.

Ironpass Electrical Maintenance Night Crew Kit#

The Ironpass night maintenance crew kit is what infrastructure looks like from the inside — functional, unglamorous, and built for crawl spaces and conduit tunnels. A matte-finish hard hat in yellow with a mounted headlamp and a flip-down face shield completes the head protection. Work gloves in arc-rated synth-leather are tucked into the left cargo pocket. The kit is clean at shift start but by 0300 it carries the smell of ozone and tunnel damp.

Ironpass Reinforced Thermal Work Shirt#

Ironthread Shelf Hauler's Full Kit#

A working rig assembled for repeated heavy labor in corrosive conditions — the kind of outfit that gets worn six days a week, washed when there's water, and repaired the same night it tears. The primary garment is a full-coverage boilersuit in heavyweight faded olive drab, the fabric stiffened from years of oil, industrial sealant, and repeated acid-rain exposure into something approaching light armor. The chest panel has a large rectangular acid-shield patch in charcoal gray, edges sealed with a bead of industrial adhesive that's cracked and re-applied so many times it forms a topographic ridge around the patch's perimeter. Both knees are likewise reinforced — the right with rubberized canvas, the left with a section of industrial conveyor belting cut to fit and secured with heavy rivets. The suit's left sleeve has been cut away at the shoulder and replaced with a chrome-compatible open channel — the wearer has a partial arm augmentation, and the channel is lined with a strip of anti-friction neoprene to prevent the chrome edge from catching on fabric. Beneath the suit, a compression underlayer in gray spandex-blend manages sweat and minor impact. Over the suit in cold conditions, a quilted over-vest in faded black adds thermal mass, its front closure a row of industrial snaps, two of which are mismatched replacements. Boots are heavy-duty, triple-resoled Shelf work boots, the uppers stitched with waxed cord in three different colors where seams have been re-done, the toe box packed with a steel plate cut from a sheet of scrap. A wide back-support belt in reinforced nylon completes the lower kit. The face is partially protected by a half-mask respirator in scuffed gray plastic, worn around the neck when not in use, its filter cartridge visibly old and marked with a hand-scratched date.

Ironveil Chrome-Scrap Street Set#

This outfit is where Shelf survival meets the aesthetic of the aug-yards — the salvage zones where stripped chrome and discarded cyberware get broken down for parts. The wearer has built their look around that world deliberately. A close-fitting long-sleeve shirt in dark graphite, made from a heavy thermal weave with aug-channel seams running along both arms — the channels are empty, not functional, but the shirt was built for chrome-users and found its way down to the Shelf. Over it hangs a sleeveless vest constructed from layered strips of salvaged materials: sections of conveyor belt rubber, cut canvas, pieces of what was once a ballistic panel, all stitched and riveted together into a rough asymmetric armor-vest that sits heavier on the left side. Salvaged chrome components — a single non-functional forearm housing stripped of its internals, worn as a bracer on the right arm; a defunct sensor ring worn as a thick wrist cuff on the left — accessorize without augmenting, a visual claim on a world that's financially out of reach. Straight-leg trousers in charcoal industrial denim, the right knee blown out and re-patched with black rubber, are tucked into mid-calf lace-up boots with thick composite soles, the leather upper cracked and re-treated until it's almost matte black. A close-cropped knit beanie in faded black, hand-stitched with a small geometric pattern in rust thread at the cuff, sits low over the ears.

Ironveil Chrome-Splice Street Rig#

On the Shelf, salvaged augmentation hardware gets repurposed — not always for function, sometimes for identity. This outfit is built around that principle. The base is a sleeveless ribbed tank in dark gray thermal synth-cotton, its back cut open along the spine in a wide channel sealed with hook-and-loop closures — aug-compatible for spinal rig wearers, though this particular wearer uses the channel to route a non-functional decorative spine rail salvaged from a discarded medical-grade aug frame. The chrome piece runs from the mid-back to just below the neck, its surface scratched and dull, a few indicator lights that no longer illuminate. Over the tank, an open-front vest in black faux-leather hangs loose, its lapels weighted with salvaged circuit board fragments wired together as decorative trim — green PCB against black synthetic, soldered at the edges. The arms are bare from the shoulder, exposing a left arm with two chrome band prosthetic segments just below the elbow — functional, basic-grade, the housing scuffed and re-painted matte black with what appears to be spray paint. The right arm is fully biological, tattooed in dense black geometric patterns from wrist to shoulder that echo the circuit board trim on the vest. High-waist trousers in stiff dark indigo canvas are belted with a wide industrial webbing belt bearing five utility clips. Boots are heavy platform-soled lace-ups in black synthetic leather, the platform built up with layers of cut rubber sheeting and wrapped in black tape — DIY height, DIY intimidation. The face is half-obscured by a single-lens optical piece — not a full BCI visor, just a salvaged single ocular unit worn over the left eye, its housing cracked but the lens still tinted gold.

Ironveil Quickpeel Extraction Operative Rig#

This is the outfit of someone who expects to need a second identity before the night is over. The outer layer is a structured jacket in deep forest green with a brushed matte finish — it reads as Tier 3 business-casual at a distance, the kind of thing a mid-management logistics coordinator might wear to a site visit. The jacket's inner face is a reversed charcoal-black with minimal texture, transforming the silhouette entirely when flipped; the collar reconfigures via a hidden snap system to shift from a spread collar to a standing Mandarin style, completing the look change. Integrated along both inner breast panels are dual holster channels with polymer retention clips, and a series of six micro-pockets sized for comm gear, breach tools, and injection cartridges run along the inner hem. The trousers are deep navy with a pressed center crease — Kelvex issues them pre-creased via thermal shaping — with two cargo pockets on the thighs secured by snap flaps and subtle safety-orange reflective tape running the outer seams. A rigid belt with a stamped utility clip holds a fare-scanner holster and a folded emergency protocol card pouch. The boots are the Veldtmann Steelcap 7, standard-issue, in black with a slip-resistant tread rated for wet platform surfaces.

A Kelvex-branded navy cap with a stiff brim and ventilated crown completes the look. Neural port covers are provided as an optional accessory — small navy discs that snap over standard BCI ports to maintain the uniform's clean appearance during passenger interaction. The entire rig is aug-compatible at the collar and sleeve, with magnetic seam detachment along the left shoulder for wearers with chrome arm rigs. Everything reads crisp from fifteen meters: this is someone who represents a company, who keeps the trains moving, and who has exactly zero patience for fare evasion.

Kestrel Crop Tee#

A clean, slightly oversized crop tee cut to hit just above the hip, made from a mid-weight cotton-modal blend that drapes softly without clinging. Kestrel is a mid-tier streetwear label with roots in the Tier 3 arts district — their aesthetic is restrained, almost deliberately quiet. The tee comes in a range of muted naturals and urban greys, occasionally punctuated by a seasonal run in a saturated color. The only branding is a small embossed 'K' at the interior neckline. No logo on the outside. The hem is finished with a clean single-needle stitch.

Kestrel Tactical Conceal Vest#

A close-fitting tactical vest designed to be worn as an outer layer — not hidden under a jacket but styled to pass as a utilitarian fashion piece. The pockets are organized for specific carry: left chest for documentation, right chest for sidearm accessories, lower left for comms, lower right general.

Kova Adaptive Hoodie#

Kova is a Tier 3 label that started as a sportswear brand and has spent the last decade trying to become a lifestyle brand, with mixed success. The Adaptive Hoodie is their best-known product — a midweight pullover hoodie in a fabric that uses embedded microfibres to shift between a denser weave in cold conditions and a more open structure when body temperature rises. In practice this means the hoodie is genuinely useful across a wider temperature range than a standard fleece. The shift is subtle — not dramatic — and takes about four minutes to respond. It won't keep you warm in a Great Lakes January, but it extends the usable season significantly.

The design is clean: a front kangaroo pocket, a lined hood with a flat drawcord, and a slight drop-tail hem. It comes in seven colors, all muted. The Kova logo appears only on a small woven tab at the hem — the brand has been moving away from chest logos since 2197. Popular with people who commute on foot, students, and anyone who spends a lot of time moving between indoor and outdoor environments in variable weather.

Lazarus emergency response teams deploy to mass-casualty events, industrial accidents, and — in practice — anywhere that Lazarus has a contractual obligation to provide care, which covers a significant portion of Meridian 88's mid and lower tiers. The triage coverall is a single-piece garment in Lazarus white with high-visibility red banding at the shoulders, wrists, and ankles. The coverall is designed with full augment compatibility: dorsal panels open via breakaway seams for responders with spinal chrome, and port-access panels at the forearms allow field diagnostics through wrist-jack interfaces without removing the suit. Lazarus MedCore Surgical Scrub Set#

The MedCore scrub set is the standard surgical uniform across Lazarus-affiliated hospitals and private clinics throughout Meridian 88. The fabric is a tightly bonded synthetic-cellulose blend rated for Class 4 biohazard splash resistance, with a micro-textured surface that actively prevents bacterial adhesion through a low-level electrostatic charge sustained by the wearer's body heat. The scrubs come in Lazarus's signature pale blue-green — a color chosen in the 2140s for its effect on patient stress responses — with the Lazarus caduceus printed in white at the left shoulder. Port access panels at the forearm and neck accommodate BCI hardline connections used during augment-adjacent surgical procedures, where the surgeon's neural interface must sync with the patient's chrome.

The MedCore set is designed with geneware accommodation as a baseline feature: the waistband includes a pre-cut tail slot reinforced with sealed edging, the hood option has molded horn-clearance inserts, and the fabric's stretch coefficient is high enough to accommodate fur-bearing limbs without restricting circulation. Lazarus supplies these scrubs at subsidized rates to licensed practitioners but sells them commercially to clinics operating outside the Lazarus network — at a significantly higher markup. In underfunded Tier 1 and 2 clinics, worn-out MedCore scrubs held together with nano-adhesive patches are a common sight, second and third owners of a garment meant to last one surgical rotation.

Lazarus Synthetic Personhood Formal Witness Robe#

Lazarus produces this robe for the formal witnesses — physicians, legal advocates, and Lazarus representatives — who attend Synthetic Personhood hearings under the Meridian 88 Bioethics Tribunal framework. Lumen Adaptive Base Layer#

A close-fitting long-sleeve base layer in a smooth four-way stretch fabric that looks at first like a high-end athletic shirt — matte charcoal or slate grey, minimal seaming, a low crew neck. It fits like a second skin without compressing, and the fabric manages temperature actively: a network of phase-change micro-capsules in the weave absorbs excess body heat when you're warm and releases it when you cool down, keeping the wearer in a narrow comfort band across a wide range of ambient temperatures. Meridian Harbor Bulk Cargo Handler Suit#

Issued to bulk cargo handlers working the lower docks where freight from irradiated Great Lakes shipping lanes is offloaded and processed, this suit is a step above standard dockwear. Meridian Harbor Crane Operator Rated Jacket#

Certified for crane and heavy-lift operations at Meridian Harbor's irradiated cargo terminals, this jacket meets the MH-Rad-3 standard for incidental radiation exposure from Class 2 contaminated freight — the kind of shipping containers arriving from the Great Lakes reclamation zones and the irradiated manufacturing corridors further east. The outer shell is a lead-composite fiber weave bonded to a thermoplastic inner layer, making the jacket heavier than standard work wear but necessary for operators spending 8–12 hour shifts in proximity to hot cargo. High-vis orange panels on the shoulders and sleeves meet harbor safety requirements, and the Harborworks Collective logo — a stylized crane hook — sits on the right chest.

The jacket is designed for the physical demands of crane operation: articulated elbow panels allow full range of motion without breaking the radiation shielding, and the collar is tall and sealed with a magnetic closure that integrates with compatible respirator collars. Augmentation compatibility is a priority given the high rate of cyberware among experienced dock workers — reinforced port-access panels are standard at the wrist and forearm, and the shoulder seams are cut wide to accommodate prosthetic or enhanced arms. A dosimeter strip on the left wrist reads cumulative radiation exposure and changes color at threshold levels. Harborworks issues replacement jackets when the strip reads yellow; most workers wait until red.

Meridian Harbor Dockworker Hazard Suit#

Meridian 88's port district processes cargo from across the continental network, including sealed containers from the irradiated shipping corridors of the former mid-Atlantic coast. The Harborline Hazard Suit is the standard-issue garment for dockworkers certified to handle Tier 2 and 3 radiation-risk cargo. The exterior shell is a lead-composite-fiber weave — lighter than traditional radiation shielding by about 60%, achieved through molecular-scale lead particle distribution — combined with a chemical-resistant outer laminate rated for most industrial solvents and biological runoff. The suit is a full-body coverage design with integrated hood, sealed cuff rings for glove attachment, and a positive-pressure collar seal. Color is a distinctive deep teal, chosen for its visibility against the grey concrete and rust of dock environments, with Harborline's anchor-and-circuit logo at the back.

The suit is built for the physical demands of dock labor: articulated joints at the knee, hip, and shoulder that don't restrict movement during heavy lifting, and reinforced knee and shin panels for crane-cab climbing. BCI port access is sealed behind a twist-lock cover to maintain suit integrity. Geneware accommodation is extensive — the dock workforce has significant geneware diversity, and Harborline's design reflects this, with tail-sealed rear seams, adjustable hood geometry for horn configurations, and stretch-panel integration at the back for early wing-stage modifications. The suit requires decontamination scan after each use in Tier 2 or higher cargo zones; workers who skip this step are subject to significant fines, a rule enforced unevenly depending on shift supervisor.

Meridian Rite Ceremonial Robe#

Mirela Hand-Knit Cabled Pullover#

Not a product. A garment made by a woman named Mirela Vascanu who lives on Stack 14, Shelf-adjacent, and has been knitting since she was a child in what was once coastal Romania. She uses reclaimed wool-analog yarn — sourced from a salvage operation that pulls fibers from discarded textile waste and re-spins them — and the result is a dense, cabled pullover in creams and heathered browns that looks like something out of a different century. The cables are a specific pattern her grandmother taught her. No two are identical.

Mirela sells perhaps thirty a year, by word of mouth only. The waiting list is informal. You know someone who knows her. The sweaters are not fashionable in any conventional sense — they're too heavy, the fit is not slim — but people who own one wear it until it falls apart, and then bring the remains back to Mirela to see if the yarn can be salvaged. In a city of manufactured goods, this is the rarest possible thing: something made slowly, by one person, for no reason except that she knows how.

Mirova Coastline Rain Shell#

Meridian 88's weather comes off the lakes hard — sideways rain, wind that finds gaps in everything, cold that drops fast. The Mirova Coastline is a rain shell built for the city's actual climate by a mid-sized outerwear label that operates out of a converted warehouse in the Tier 2 port district. The shell is a three-layer bonded nylon in muted slate blue, forest green, or the perennial seller, a dark burgundy that doesn't show grime. The hood packs into the collar, the cuffs seal with velcro tabs, and the front zip is covered by a snap-close storm flap. It is not a beautiful jacket. It is a jacket that keeps you dry.

The Coastline sells well across Tier 2 and Tier 3 because it costs a reasonable amount of money and does exactly what it claims. It's the jacket you grab when the weather app says seventy percent chance of precipitation and you don't want to ruin anything better. Students wear it. Commuters wear it. Street vendors who work outdoor stalls in the transit plazas wear it. Nobody notices you wearing it, which is sometimes exactly what you want.

Myriad Collective Patchwork Varsity#

The Myriad Collective is a rotating group of textile artists and garment makers based in the Shelf's creative district — what passes for one. Nakamura-Voss NV-7 Patrol Vest#

A tactical vest worn by private security contractors and building security throughout the mid-tiers. Constructed from a dense ballistic-weave nylon with soft armor panels integrated into the front and back — rated for low-velocity rounds and blade resistance, though Nakamura-Voss is careful never to make specific performance claims in their marketing materials. MOLLE webbing runs along the chest and sides for attachment of pouches and accessories. Available in black, slate grey, and a dark navy used by several corponation security divisions.

The NV-7 is the visual shorthand for 'armed private security' throughout Meridian 88. It reads as authority in the mid-tiers and as threat in the Shelf. The soft armor panels are removable for laundering, and the vest itself is reasonably comfortable for all-day wear — a small mercy for the people who spend twelve-hour shifts in them.

Nana Kwesi's Hand-Knit Cable Pullover#

Not a brand. Not a product line. Just a sweater knitted by an elderly man named Kwesi Asamoah-Lindqvist who lives in a Tier 2 residential block in the north corridor and sells his work through a small table at the weekend market near the Halsted transit hub. Nexigen Biometric Base Layer#

Nexigen's biometric base layer looks, at first glance, like a plain fitted long-sleeve shirt in charcoal or white. The fabric is a proprietary stretch-composite that sits close to the skin and breathes well enough to wear all day without discomfort. It's only when you look at the collar seam that you notice the thin embedded sensor strip — a continuous loop of conductive thread that reads skin temperature, perspiration rate, and heart rate variability, syncing passively to a paired BCI or personal device.

The data it generates is unobtrusive and continuous — not a medical device, but a wellness layer. It tells you when you're running hot before you feel it, tracks stress markers across a workday, and can be set to alert on anomalies. Nexigen sells these primarily to Tier 3 and 4 professionals who want the data without wearing a visible device. The shirt is comfortable enough that many people forget it's doing anything. That comfort is, depending on your perspective, the feature or the concern.

Nexkin Adaptive Undershirt#

A form-fitting crew-neck undershirt from Nexkin — a Tier 3/4 technical apparel label — made from a proprietary stretch-weave fabric embedded with a passive thermal regulation mesh. The mesh doesn't require power; it's a phase-change material woven directly into the fabric that absorbs heat when the wearer runs hot and releases it when they cool down. The effect is subtle and real: not air conditioning, not heating, just a persistent effort to keep the wearer somewhere near comfortable. The shirt itself is seamless at the shoulders and sides, with flat-locked seams everywhere else.

It's designed to be worn under other garments and is almost aggressively uninteresting to look at — available in black, white, and a medium grey. The value is entirely in the wear. Tier 3 office workers, people with augments that run hot, and anyone who spends long hours in climate-inconsistent environments (construction, field work, transit) wear these as a quiet investment in their own comfort. Some Tier 4 professionals wear them under suits without mentioning it.

A floor-length cloak in matte black that does not stay matte black. Nullweave Diplomatic Formal Gown#

Nullweave's diplomatic line was developed in response to a specific problem: formal garments that carry too many signals. Corporate colors, cultural insignia, tier-display materials, affiliation badges — in high-stakes inter-corponation or inter-faction diplomatic settings, every visual cue is a variable that can derail a conversation before it starts. The Diplomatic Formal Gown resolves this through deliberate neutrality. The fabric is a cool-toned off-white silk-analog that has been engineered to read as neither warm nor cold under any standard interior lighting spectrum. The silhouette is conservative and globally non-specific — no cut that reads as culturally affiliated, no ornamentation that signals anything. Privacy-weave lining is standard. BCI-responsive elements are absent by design.

The gown accommodates augmentations at the shoulder and spine via flush magnetic seaming, and a standard tail accommodation is available. It is not a beautiful garment in any exciting sense. It is a garment engineered to create no friction, to give observers nothing to react to, to allow the person wearing it to be evaluated on what they say rather than what they wear. In certain rooms, that is worth considerably more than beauty.

Nullweave Diplomatic Formal Suit#

Nullweave Tier-4 Chrome-Display Office Suit#

For the augmented professional who has stopped hiding their chrome and started wearing it as a credential. The Nullweave Tier-4 Chrome-Display Office Suit is cut from a deep navy stretch-woven fabric with a matte finish that reads as formal from across a meeting room but moves like a second skin. The jacket is structured at the shoulder but open-seamed along the left sleeve from mid-bicep to wrist — a deliberate aug-display cut that lets chrome forearm and wrist installations be seen without removing the jacket. The open seam is finished with a brushed gunmetal trim that echoes the chrome it frames, creating the impression that the suit was designed around the augmentation rather than adapted for it. It was. The right sleeve is fully closed, traditional, creating an asymmetry that reads as intentional style rather than accommodation. Underneath, a fitted Nullweave mock-neck base shirt in slate-grey with a rear neural port channel — a clean slot at the base of the collar that sits open, allowing BCI port access without disturbing the shirt's line. Trousers are slim-tapered in matching navy stretch-woven, with a hidden inner-thigh seam channel for lower-limb chrome routing, sealed with a micro-zip along the inner leg. Footwear is a pair of matte-black side-zip ankle boots with a reinforced toe cap — practical, grounded, and just formatted enough to pass a Tier 4 dress code audit. The aug-display cut telegraphs a specific message in corporate culture: this person's chrome is not a disability accommodation, it is a qualification.

NutriRoute All-Season Cart Stand Operator Kit#

The working uniform of the street food economy — practical, presentable, and built to survive a fourteen-hour shift at a corner cart through rain, heat, and the occasional chemical fog rolling off the elevated transit lines above. The primary piece is a collarless canvas work apron in deep slate grey, mid-thigh length, with a wide bib, three front pockets (one for order slips, one for payment hardware, one for a folded cloth), and the NutriRoute licensing logo embroidered at the bib in rust-orange thread — marking the wearer as operating under a franchise arrangement rather than fully independent. Beneath the apron, a long-sleeve moisture-wicking crew shirt in burnt sienna with a simple stand collar, worn tucked. Trousers are straight-leg charcoal synth-cotton with a comfortable high rise, flat front, and two deep hip pockets. Footwear is a cushioned slip-resistant clog in matte black with a wide toe box and a closed heel — designed for standing. A lightweight packable rain shell in translucent grey with orange reflective seam tape hangs from a hook on the cart when not in use, pulled on when weather turns.

NutriRoute Cart Vendor All-Season Stand Kit#

The full working uniform of a NutriRoute licensed street cart vendor — one of the Circuit tier's most visible workers, stationed at transit hubs, factory gates, and corridor intersections through all weather. The foundation is a pair of straight-cut black synth-cotton trousers with deep side pockets and a reinforced inner-thigh panel for long hours of standing and squatting. The primary layer is a NutriRoute branded quarter-zip pullover in safety orange with a white NutriRoute wordmark across the chest and a QR patch on the left sleeve that links to the cart's live menu — updated remotely by the vendor. The quarter-zip collar can be pulled high against wind; the cuffs are tight-knit to keep out cold without hampering hand movement. Over it in cold weather: a padded gilet in charcoal with a high mock-neck collar, multiple zippered chest pockets for holding Quanta-chip payment terminals, and hi-vis silver strips at the shoulder seams.

On the head: a NutriRoute-branded mesh-back cap in orange and black, the brim curved and worn low against sun or drizzle. A full-length black synthetic-rubber apron ties at the waist and chest, covering the front of the outfit during service — stain-resistant, wipe-clean, with a front kangaroo pocket holding order-slip printouts and a pen-stylus. Footwear is a pair of Foundry Broadfoot Work Sneakers in black — cushioned for standing shifts, oil-resistant sole, slightly scuffed from daily use. The vendor's hands are bare for service speed, knuckles often chapped from cold. A small bioluminescent flower sticker — personal, not corporate — is stuck to the inside brim of the cap, glowing faintly blue: the only soft thing in the whole outfit.

Odeya Blouse (Adire Print)#

A loose, flowing blouse cut from a medium-weight fabric printed in a modern interpretation of traditional Yoruba adire resist-dyeing: deep indigo ground with irregular white geometric resists — circles, broken lines, scatter patterns — that look hand-done because they were, at least in the original design that the print is derived from. The blouse is popular across Tiers 2 through 4, worn by people who appreciate heritage design and by people who simply think it's beautiful without knowing its context. Both are fine.

Okafor Systems ThermoShell Parka#

A heavyweight hooded parka designed for sustained cold-weather exposure, sold primarily through Okafor Systems' industrial supply division but widely available in Tier 2 and Tier 3 outlets. When the lakefront wind drops to minus fifteen and the spray is coming off the water, this is what keeps you alive.

Oluwa & Park Adire Varsity#

Oluwa & Park is a street label that came out of the Tier 2 arts corridor in the old Wicker Park footprint, founded by a Nigerian-Korean design collective who wanted to make things that looked like where they came from. The Adire Varsity takes the classic varsity silhouette — wool body, leather sleeves, ribbed collar and cuffs — and rebuilds it in indigo-dyed adire fabric for the body panels, the patterns varying batch to batch because the dyeing process is partially intentional and partially not. The leather sleeves are in a deep oxblood, hand-stitched. No team name. No mascot. The only branding is a small woven label inside the collar with a circular mark that regulars recognize.

This jacket moves through the mid tiers and punches up. Tier 3 buyers find it at the label's single physical shop; Tier 4 buyers have started hunting it through resellers and paying double. The Shelf knows it too — not to wear, usually, but to move. A genuine Adire Varsity in good condition is currency in certain social circles. The fact that it's beautiful and the patterns are unrepeatable makes it the kind of thing people hold onto.

Oma Nkechi's Stitchwork Pullover#

Everyone in the Tier 2 Aboagye-Lindqvist neighborhood knows someone who has one of these. Nkechi Aboagye, who goes by Oma Nkechi to the block, has been knitting and selling pullovers from her apartment on the 14th floor of the Greaves stack for twenty-three years. The yarn is a blend she sources herself — recycled wool-analog, some real merino she trades favors for, occasionally a fiber that shifts color slightly with body heat that she picks up from a supplier she won't name. Each sweater has her signature asymmetrical ribbing at the hem and a different front panel motif — geometric, often Akan-derived, occasionally incorporating Nordic grid patterns from her late husband's family.

They are not cheap for the neighborhood — Φ65 to Φ90 depending on the yarn — but they last a decade of hard wear and she repairs them for free. Owning one marks you as someone who lives in or is connected to a specific few blocks of Tier 2 Chicago-North. It's a geographic and social belonging, knitted in.

Orison Brushed Flannel Shirt#

Orison is a workwear-adjacent label that occupies the comfortable middle ground between functional and presentable — the kind of brand that outfitters stock alongside hiking gear and hardware stores carry alongside work gloves. The Brushed Flannel Shirt is a long-sleeve button-front in a medium-weight brushed flannel, cut generously through the shoulders and chest to allow movement without pulling. The plaid pattern runs in a traditional block check — a rotation of four colorways each season, always including a dark red/black and a navy/forest green. Two chest pockets with button flaps. This shirt has no technology in it. It is flannel. It is warm in the way flannel is warm — not aggressively, not technically, just reliably. People wear it open over a thermal layer on job sites, or buttoned up to the second button at a casual dinner, or thrown over a tank top on a cool morning before the temperature decides what it wants to be. It is the kind of shirt that appears in the background of every social tier from Tier 2 through Tier 3 without calling attention to itself. That is its entire point.

Orvana Geneware Executive Presence Suit#

A Tier 5 bespoke suit designed for the growing population of Spire executives who have undergone significant geneware modification and refuse to let it diminish their sartorial authority. The jacket is a fluid-structured double-breasted cut by Orvana's atelier division, executed in 'luminwave silk-wool' — a fabric that shifts between a warm charcoal and a deep amber-bronze depending on the angle of light, achieved through a nano-fiber orientation process that takes roughly four hours per panel to set. The rear of the jacket is cut in an asymmetric drape rather than a standard back panel, opening into a wide, structured wing-slit: two reinforced channels of matching luminwave fabric that frame non-functional decorative wings or small functional geneware wing structures without compressing the membrane. The slit edges are finished with a thin line of brushed gold-alloy trim that catches light at the perimeter of any wing display. The tail accommodation is built into the trouser: a high-waisted wide-leg pant in matching luminwave with a rear pleat system that opens into a clean, fully finished tail-vent, the opening framed in the same gold-alloy trim as the jacket wing-slit, creating a deliberate visual continuity between the geneware accommodations as design elements rather than afterthoughts.

The shirt beneath is an Orvana Silk-Analog Drape Blouse in deep ivory with a draped open collar that sits wide at the sternum, accommodating any bioluminescent skin modifications at the chest and throat without coverage that would obscure them. Footwear is the Caelum IX Pressure-Form Dress Heel in matte black with a gold-alloy cap-toe, adding height without instability. The BCI neural port at the base of the skull is framed by the jacket's collar, which has been cut with a precise oval relief that exposes the port as an intentional detail — a polished chrome ring trim around the opening making it look like a piece of architectural hardware. This outfit does not hide what the wearer is. It builds a room around it.

Orvana Occasion Gown — Tail-Vent Standard#

Orvana's accessible line — distinct from their Spire couture — is designed for Tier 3 buyers who want genuine tailoring at a price that doesn't require financing. The Occasion Gown is floor-length, cut in a silk-analog that holds color well and resists static cling in the charged air of most Meridian indoor venues. The Tail-Vent Standard variant includes a structured rear panel that splits cleanly from mid-hip to hem, with internal tension bands that keep the split closed when standing and open naturally under movement. It accommodates most TESSERA standard-issue geneware tails without bunching or binding.

Orvana offers the gown in twelve colorways and four standard geneware configurations: tail-vent, wing-slit back, horn-clearance hood attachment, and standard. Custom configurations are available for an additional Φ40–Φ80. The construction is clean and the fit is reliable. It is not a statement piece — it is a dress that works, that lasts, and that doesn't make the wearer think about it during the event.

Orvex Tactical MA-2 Bomber#

A militarized update of the classic MA-1 bomber silhouette, manufactured by Orvex for the private security and civilian tactical markets. Private site guards buy it for function; younger residents buy it for the silhouette and the association. The jacket carries no overt branding — just a small woven label inside the collar. On the Shelf, a secondhand MA-2 is considered a score.

Orvex Thermal Shell#

A hard-shell rain jacket designed for the Great Lakes corridor's legendary wet seasons — the weeks in March and October when the lake pushes cold horizontal rain through every gap in the city's windbreak towers. It packs into its own chest pocket.

Orvex is a Tier 3 outdoor gear brand that sells primarily to commuters and light outdoors enthusiasts. The Shell comes in muted earth tones and a few brighter safety-adjacent colors. It's unassuming and works exactly as advertised. People who spend a lot of time outside — courier cyclists, construction supervisors, field technicians — own at least one.

Oxweld ChemBarrier Overcoat#

A long, stiff-shouldered overcoat in industrial yellow-tan, manufactured specifically for Shelf residents and Tier 2 workers who live near chemical processing zones, waste corridors, or the old industrial lakefront. The outer shell is a laminated multi-layer barrier fabric rated for splash resistance against a documented list of common corridor contaminants — sulfuric compounds, petrochemical residue, certain industrial solvents. It is not a full hazmat suit. It is what people wear when they cannot afford a full hazmat suit but still need to walk home through a place that smells wrong. The coat reaches the ankles, has sealed cuffs that can be cinched over gloves, and a high collar with a filtration-compatible face seal along the upper edge.

Oxweld is a Tier 1 to 2 corponation subsidiary — technically a safety equipment manufacturer, not a fashion brand — and their overcoats are sold in bulk through company stores, Shelf distribution points, and licensed resellers near industrial zones. They are ugly. They are effective within their rating. The lining is a rough cotton-poly that chafes in cold weather and the seams are utilitarian at best. But when the eastern wind comes off the old industrial channel and the air tastes metallic, you want one of these between you and whatever is in that air.

Patchskin Drift Coat#

A long, dramatic coat that is less a single garment than a living document of the Shelf — every panel a different salvaged fabric, stitched and fused into a floor-length silhouette that somehow holds together. Dark panels of industrial rubber sheeting alternate with sections of waxed sailcloth, synthetic suede in faded ochre, and several squares of what was once a high-visibility vest, now so oxidized it reads as deep amber rather than yellow. The lining is a quilt of mismatched thermal emergency blankets, crinkled and reflective on the inside, visible through the wide lapels. The coat closes with a mismatched run of fasteners — two toggles, three large snaps, and a length of paracord threaded through grommets at the center. Beneath it, a long-sleeve thermal undershirt in off-white sits tucked into straight-cut trousers in deep charcoal that have been hemmed unevenly — one leg slightly shorter than the other after a repair. The trouser knees are patched with iron-on synthetic leather. Feet are in rubber overshoes — bright orange, institutional, clearly salvaged from a flood-response kit — worn over a thin pair of insulated socks. On the head, a deep-crown beanie in black wool-synth, hand-darned at the brim with mismatched thread in three colors. Hands are bare except for a single fingerless compression glove on the left hand. One ear carries a salvaged audio driver — a small speaker housing repurposed as an earring, trailing a thin wire that disappears into the coat's collar.

Patchwork Collective Scrap Tee#

There is no single Patchwork Collective Scrap Tee — each one is unique. They're assembled by the loose network of Shelf sewers and textile scavengers who trade under the Patchwork Collective name, stitching together salvaged fabric scraps, old band shirts, industrial textile remnants, and whatever else is available into something wearable. The base structure is usually a simple crew-neck tee shape, but the surface is a map of wherever the fabric came from — a stripe of Ghanaian kente-print synth cotton next to a panel of faded logistics-corp khaki next to a scrap of what might have been a child's blanket.

They're sold at Shelf markets, traded between residents, and occasionally show up in Tier 2 neighborhoods where people buy them as art objects. On the Shelf, they're just clothes — warm enough, structurally sound, repaired and re-repaired. The stitching is sometimes crude and sometimes extraordinarily fine, depending on who made it. No two are the same.

Pelikan Hi-Vis Safety Shell#

There is nothing subtle about this jacket and that is entirely the point. The Pelikan Hi-Vis Safety Shell is a Class 3 high-visibility rain jacket in ANSI-equivalent fluorescent yellow-green, with retroreflective silver tape at the chest, back, and arms in the standard chevron pattern. It is a lightweight shell, wind- and water-resistant, with a mesh lining and a hood that adjusts with a single cord. The Pelikan logo is small and on the chest. Everything else is light.

This is the jacket of infrastructure workers, road crews, site safety monitors, and dock workers across the Great Lakes corridor. It is also worn by anyone who needs to be seen in the dark — Shelf residents navigating dangerous transit routes sometimes wear hi-vis ironically or earnestly, as visibility is survival in certain parts of the city. Pelikan makes good shells at a working price. The reflective tape on this model catches light from a hundred meters.

PolyRoute Delivery Driver Weathershell#

PolyRoute is one of M88's dominant last-mile delivery networks, and the Weathershell is what their drivers wear through the city's full meteorological range — acid-tinged lake squalls, the deep cold of Great Lakes winters, and the wet heat that settles over the megacity's lower districts in summer. The jacket is a three-layer construction: an outer shell of hydrophobic ripstop that sheds water and resists the mild chemical content of Meridian 88's precipitation, a thermal-regulating mid-layer that adjusts insulation based on exertion level, and a moisture-wicking inner face. A GPS-conductive thread network runs through the jacket's left sleeve, connecting to a wrist-worn routing display that pulls live delivery manifests, traffic data, and route optimization from PolyRoute's logistics AI. The jacket includes a chest-mounted scanner holster for package verification hardware. BCI-compatible collar port allows hands-free navigation for drivers with neural interface setups. The Weathershell is geneware-tolerant at the back and waist — tail accommodation gussets are standard, and the hood has adjustable side clearance for ear configurations. PolyRoute drivers are contractors, not employees, which means the jacket is technically a rental deducted from earnings — a financial arrangement that generates significant resentment among the workforce.

Rennick Leatherworks Café Racer#

Rennick Leatherworks is a one-person operation — or close to it — running out of a workshop in the mid-Tier 2 district, making motorcycle and riding jackets from genuine and synthetic leather in the old tradition. The Café Racer is a fitted, hip-length moto jacket with a snap-off collar, asymmetric zip front, and two hand-slash pockets. The leather is full-grain bovine hide treated with a proprietary wax blend that makes it water-resistant and gives it a deep, dark sheen. The lining is quilted satin-analog in burgundy or black.

People who actually ride motorcycles in Meridian 88's traffic corridors wear it. People who do not ride also wear it, which Rennick finds mildly annoying.

Revv Moto Blackline Jacket#

Revv Moto is a street-level motorcycle gear brand that operates out of the Tier 2 transport district, building jackets for people who actually ride in the city rather than for people who want to look like they do. The Blackline is their flagship — a full-grain synthetic leather jacket in flat black with minimal stitching detail, a slightly asymmetric zip closure, and removable CE-rated armor inserts at the shoulders, elbows, and a spine channel at the back. The collar is medium height and zips fully closed against wind. The lining is a quilted black nylon that can be removed in warmer months. It fits close without being restrictive, and the shoulder seams are positioned forward to allow for riding posture without binding.

Riders across Tier 2 and Tier 3 buy these. The Blackline has also developed a following among people who don't ride but want the silhouette and the armor without the price of the premium brands. On the street it reads as competence — this is the jacket of someone who knows something about moving through the city fast and coming out the other side. The chrome-free hardware is a deliberate choice; Revv Moto's founder has a well-known position on unnecessary flash.

Ringo Broadcast Field Technician Vest#

Ringo's field broadcast technicians — the crew running cameras, signal repeaters, and live-feed rigs for everything from sponsored sports events to political press junkets — wear this vest as their standard on-site identifier. Built from a durable ripstop nylon in Ringo's electric red, the vest carries 14 external pockets of varying size calibrated for broadcast hardware: signal boosters, battery packs, lens filters, and interface cables all have designated homes. The Ringo 'R' logo in reflective white sits on the front and back, making crew identifiable in crowded or chaotic environments. Interior mesh lining keeps the vest breathable during long outdoor shoots.

The vest is designed to layer over personal clothing rather than replace it, which means it accommodates almost any body type or modification without manufacturer adjustment — the front closes with a wide-gap magnetic buckle system that clears most chest-mounted chrome, and the back panel is split to accommodate wing stubs or dorsal geneware modifications. A passive signal-routing harness built into the lining allows the wearer's BCI to interface directly with compatible Ringo broadcast hardware. Crew members have a complicated relationship with the vest: it marks you as essential on set, but it also makes you invisible to the talent and the executives who pretend the broadcast happens by itself.

Ringo Media Group Field Press Vest#

Ringo's on-ground media personnel — the reporters, fixers, and content capture crews who work outside the studio — wear the Field Press Vest, a garment that sits at the intersection of corporate branding and practical journalism. The vest is constructed from a medium-weight weather-resistant ripstop in Ringo's signature electric yellow, with the Ringo wordmark in bold black across the back and a smaller logo at the left chest. Twelve external pockets accommodate capture equipment, data chips, external BCI relay hardware, and backup power cells. The vest is not armored, but it is treated with a visual-prominence coating that makes it highly visible on camera and in crowd footage — a deliberate design choice, as Ringo's field staff rely on their recognizability as press for a degree of social protection in volatile coverage zones.

The vest includes a BCI-sync port at the collar that connects to Ringo's proprietary LiveStream infrastructure, allowing field personnel to push content directly to Ringo's broadcast networks without local processing. A passive GPS weave tracks field crew positions and feeds to the Ringo logistics desk. The vest is explicitly not designed for hostile environments — Ringo's liability documentation is extremely clear that it confers no ballistic or chemical protection — but field crews working Shelf assignments frequently modify their vests with third-party trauma inserts, a practice Ringo officially discourages and unofficially depends on. Geneware accommodation is minimal; the vest is cut for a standard human silhouette, and crew members with significant modifications often find it ill-fitting.

Rourke & Sable Lambskin Moto Jacket#

Rustbloom Scrapper's Wrapped Street Set#

Built around a long wrap-style top derived from a West African agbada pattern — but executed in salvaged industrial linen dyed unintentionally rust-brown by repeated acid-rain exposure, the original white fiber still visible at protected inner seams. The wrap is fixed at the shoulder with a repurposed industrial cable clamp, its chrome surface dulled by grinding but still catching light. Beneath it, a tight ribbed turtleneck in faded black synth-cotton covers the neck and wrists. The lower half is a pair of wide-leg work trousers in stiff dark brown canvas, cuffed at the ankle and belted with a length of woven nylon strap threaded through a buckle salvaged from a harness rig. Along the outer seam of each leg runs a vertical strip of reflective tape — partly for visibility in unlit tunnels, partly just because the wearer found a roll of it and it stuck. Feet are wrapped first in thick wool socks, then pushed into ankle boots resoled with layered conveyor belt rubber, the upper leather cracked to a beautiful dark-map pattern and treated with rendered fat to keep the cracks from spreading. Around the neck hangs a cord of braided copper wire strung with three salvaged BCI interface pins — non-functional, worn as jewelry — and a flat disc of oxidized steel etched by hand with a geometric pattern. Hair is wrapped in a tight cloth band cut from the same rust-brown industrial linen as the top wrap.

Rustwater Layering Rig#

A full-body survival stack built for the Shelf's acid-laced downpours. The outermost layer is a knee-length anorak cut from salvaged industrial tarp material — once corporate safety-orange, now faded to a streaky rust-and-cream, with mismatched patches of rubberized canvas heat-bonded over the shoulders and collar where the acid eats fastest. A battered wide-brim hat in waxed cotton, stained dark at the crown, completes the silhouette.

Ryokan Ashgrey Slub Henley#

Ryokan is a small-batch label operating out of a workshop in the Midmarket district, making garments that sit at the intersection of Japanese workwear restraint and the kind of soft, worn-in quality associated with American heritage clothing — a combination that feels natural in a city where cultural boundaries dissolved long ago. The Ashgrey Slub Henley is their signature piece: a three-button henley in a slubby cotton-analog that has an irregular, slightly textured surface suggesting handmade without claiming it. The fit is relaxed through the chest and shoulders, slightly tapered at the waist. The grey is not a clean grey — it has depth, warmth, the quality of something that was once another color and has arrived here through time.

It's the kind of shirt that people who care about clothes recognize immediately and people who don't care about clothes never notice. The stitching is tight, the seams are clean, the collar won't deform. Ryokan makes two hundred of these per season. They sell out in days. No advertising.

Sable & Fork Food Service Uniform Set#

Sable & Fork is the dominant supplier of food service uniforms across Meridian 88's restaurant and catering industry, covering everything from Tier 2 canteens to Tier 4 corporate dining facilities. The standard set includes a double-breasted chef's coat, work trousers, and an apron, all constructed from a heat-resistant synthetic-cotton blend rated to sustained exposure at 280°C without degradation. The coat is white with black piping at the collar and cuff — a deliberate neutral that allows restaurants to add their own branding through embroidery or heat-transfer patches. The apron is a heavier canvas weave with a grease-resistant coating that repels most organic and synthetic cooking oils; it can be wiped clean during a shift and machine-washed at the end. The trouser design includes wide-leg construction to avoid heat trapping near open flame or induction surfaces.

Sable & Fork's geneware accommodation is notably thorough for food service wear, driven by the reality that kitchen workforces in M88 are highly diverse. The coat includes a rear yoke panel that opens for tail clearance, the collar sits low enough to avoid friction with common neck augments, and the hat options include a structured toque with horn-clearance inserts as well as a close-fit net cap designed for fur-bearing head configurations — both rated as equivalent hygienic coverage under Meridian 88's food safety code. The uniform set is priced at the lower end of Sable & Fork's range; higher-tier establishments typically order the structured Maison line, but the standard set is what keeps M88's food industry running.

Sable Freight Long-Haul Cab Driver's Road Rig#

Independent long-haul freight cab operators — the ones running Sable Freight contracts through the M88 outer corridors, acid-rain bypasses, and inter-sector cargo routes — put together a rig that works for sixteen hours in a cab seat and doesn't fall apart when they have to get out and deal with a breakdown at 3 AM on an elevated causeway. The trousers are Goretek cargo-cut in washed navy, broken in soft over years, with reinforced seat and inner thigh for long sits, a wide waistband that doesn't dig during extended driving, and cargo pockets on both thighs sealed with snap-buttons. A wide webbing belt in black carries a compact multi-tool and a key fob clip. The upper layer starts with an Ironpass-style heavy thermal work shirt in faded olive — flannel-weight synth-cotton, chest pockets with button closures, rolled-up sleeves almost always, with a Sable Freight contractor patch heat-pressed to the left sleeve upper arm. Over this, when out of the cab, goes a quilted vest in dark charcoal with a stand collar — no sleeves, allowing full arm mobility for cargo strapping and vehicle checks, with a large interior pocket on the left breast for a route tablet. Boots are mid-cut moto-style in worn black synth-leather with a side zip, thick lug sole, and a reinforced toe — not steel-capped, prioritizing comfort for the long sit over full safety rating. A worn baseball-style cap in Sable Freight charcoal-grey with a battered brim completes the head, usually worn front-forward, neural port at the rear left accommodated by a stitched-open eyelet in the cap's rear adjustment band.

Sable Freight Longhaul Flannel#

A heavyweight flannel shirt in a traditional two-color plaid — navy and grey, or rust and charcoal — with a full button front and a chest pocket on each side. The fabric is a brushed synthetic-wool that has nearly the same hand as real flannel but doesn't compress or mat with repeated washing. Reinforced at the collar, cuffs, and pocket corners. Cut generously through the chest and shoulders to allow layering over a thermal base. Long tails can be tucked or worn out.

Sable Freight issues these as optional cold-weather supplement to standard uniform sets, but they've migrated well beyond the logistics workforce. They're durable, warm, and cost less than most of their competitors. You'll find them on dock workers layered over Ironpass thermals, on Tier 2 families at weekend markets, on Shelf residents who acquired them secondhand, and on Tier 3 people who like the aesthetic and appreciate that the quality is real. The Sable Freight logo tag is small and easily removed.

Sableworks Independent Dock & Freight Hauler Set#

A self-assembled working kit favored by independent dock laborers and freight haulers who contract shift-to-shift at Meridian Harbor's lower berths rather than drawing a corponation wage. The core garment is a heavyweight charcoal synth-denim overall with brass-toned rivets at stress points, bib-front chest pockets with button flaps, and a full back panel cut wide to accommodate spinal rigs and dorsal augmentation harnesses — a long zipper runs the spine from tailbone to collar, allowing a rig to be donned or removed without stripping the whole garment. The bib straps are reinforced nylon webbing adjustable for different torso depths. Beneath the overall, a burnt-orange thermal long-sleeve with raglan seams provides wind resistance; its cuffs are tight-knit to seal against the bib hem. A wide-brimmed oilskin work hat in dark brown sheds acid-rain and harbor spray. Hands are covered by cut-resistant synth-leather work gloves with knuckle padding, left thumb and index finger tipped in conductive material for touchscreen interaction. Footwear is a pair of Dockmaster Deepwade Boots, calf-high with composite toe caps and anti-slip hull-grade soles.

Nothing on this outfit carries a corponation logo — a deliberate choice. Independent haulers often sew a single personal identifier: a small embroidered sigil or color-coded shoulder tab that marks their crew affiliation to other independents without advertising it to corporate port managers. The overall has been patched at the left knee with a slightly mismatched charcoal panel, a common repair that reads as lived-in competence rather than poverty.

Scaleback Recon Layering Set#

Lean and functional, this outfit is assembled for someone who needs to move fast, carry nothing unnecessary, and still survive the Shelf's worst conditions. The top layer is a close-cut moto-style jacket in salvaged coated nylon — originally black, now a streaky charcoal with surface cracking along the creases — with a short stand collar and asymmetric zipper, the pull replaced with a length of wire twisted into a loop. The jacket's back panel has been slit vertically along the center seam and re-closed with an industrial zipper, creating a channel that accommodates a spinal aug rig: the wearer's chrome spinal column reinforcement is visible through the gap when the back zipper is cracked open, catching light in silver-grey segments. The jacket's interior is lined with a layer of aluminized mylar cut from emergency blankets, adding thermal retention without bulk. Underneath is a fitted long-sleeve rashguard in dark olive, the collar high enough to cover the lower neck ports of the spinal rig. Below the waist, slim tactical trousers in faded black with articulated knees — clearly salvaged from a Circuit-level security uniform, the original patch locations now lighter squares where insignia were removed. A slim profile boot in synthetic leather rises to mid-calf, side-zip, with a thin lug sole; the right boot has a narrow sheath sewn into the inner shaft. On the head, a close-cropped cap in the same faded black as the trousers, worn low. Around the neck, a thin lanyard holds a cracked plastic ID card — the text worn off, the photo unrecognizable, kept for reasons the wearer hasn't explained to anyone.

Scrap-Stitch Patchwork Tank#

Not a product with a brand — a category of garment that exists across the Shelf wherever people have access to a needle, thread, and discarded fabric. This particular style has emerged as something almost coherent: a tank top constructed from three to six different fabric panels, each from a different source — a piece of a Caldero thermal, a strip of printed synthwool, a section of what might have been a corporate uniform, all sewn together with visible stitching in mismatched thread colors. Some makers reinforce stress points with salvaged metal rings or knotted cord. Some add patches — hand-drawn logos, strips of reflective tape, safety pins through the hem.

What distinguishes a good scrap-stitch tank from a bad one is the stitching and the color sense. The best ones show a genuine eye for what goes together. They circulate by gift and trade as often as sale. Wearing one is a declaration of where you come from that no amount of money can buy, which is why Tier 3 and 4 youth occasionally try, and why it always reads wrong when they do.

Shelf Ghost Tank#

Not a manufactured item — a category. On the Shelf, a Ghost Tank is any sleeveless top that's been stripped, cut, bleached, painted, and re-stitched until its original identity is gone. The one in your hand might have started as a Meridian Transit Authority uniform, a Tokusen Industries promo shirt, or a kids' athletic set. Now it's been cut at the shoulders, the neckline widened with a blade, and stenciled with a crow skull or a glitch-art pattern in white house pigment. The hem is raw or knotted. Maybe a strip of reflective salvage tape runs diagonal across the back.

They sell in clusters at Shelf market stalls — three for Φ12, or individually from someone who takes their customization seriously enough to charge Φ18 for a specific piece. No two are identical. Wearing one is a statement that you came from somewhere specific and didn't bother to hide it.

Shelf Patchwork Tank (Scavenged)#

Not a manufactured item — this is something built from nothing. A tank top assembled from three or four mismatched fabric sources: a section of old corporate uniform fabric (the logo partially burned or bleached out), a strip of fluorescent mesh from a construction vest, and a back panel that might be repurposed synth-bag material. Siltframe Deep-Pocket Infiltration Rig#

Built around a long overshirt in silt-green matte ripstop — not a jacket, not quite a coat, landing at mid-thigh — this rig succeeds by looking like it belongs everywhere and nowhere specific. The overshirt has fourteen pockets total, only four of which are externally visible; the rest are internal panel pockets accessed through slotted seams along the side chest, inner hem, and a full-width lower-back channel designed to double as a flat equipment carry. The fabric is woven with an irregular charcoal grid pattern that breaks up body outline on low-resolution surveillance cameras. Underneath, a close-fit base layer in near-black burgundy thermal-weave manages temperature and provides a second surface of scanner-disrupting material. The trousers are slim-cut in dark storm-grey with aug-routing channels along the outer thigh — reinforced conduit seams that guide power cables from leg prosthetics or chrome augmentation without pinching or snagging. A detachable cargo panel can be added or removed from the left thigh via snap-bar. Footwear is a mid-ankle boot in dark green synthetic suede over a rubberized low-profile sole, with magnetic-close side panels instead of laces — fast on, fast off. A narrow hood is stored collapsed inside the overshirt's rear collar and deploys in two seconds, covering the neck and the back of the skull without obscuring peripheral vision.

Slagside Patched Work Shirt#

Not a product — a practice. The Slagside Patched Work Shirt is a Shelf tradition: a long-sleeve button-front work shirt, usually a dead brand or salvaged industrial uniform top, repaired and personalized until the original garment is more patch than shirt. Common base garments include old Solberg-Maru uniform shirts, defunct corponation maintenance coverall tops, and whatever durable synth-fabric shirts cycle through the Shelf's secondhand stalls. Patches are anything that holds — fabric scraps, adhesive repair tape in contrasting colors, heat-fused synthetic leather squares, embroidered panels traded between neighbors.

No two are alike. They're worn as a point of identity: in a district where you can't afford to look like anything, you make yourself look like something. Some Shelf residents spend months on a single shirt, treating it as an ongoing project. Others are purely functional — rip, patch, wear. The name 'Slagside' comes from one of the Shelf's most densely populated industrial zones, but the practice is city-wide.

Slagside Rivet-Crown Face Shield#

Hammered from salvaged industrial press plates and bent into rough face coverage, the Rivet-Crown is a Shelf staple — ugly, functional, and unmistakably hand-made. Mismatched rivet heads hold overlapping panels of grey and rust-orange scrap steel, with a scratched polycarbonate visor strip salvaged from a defunct transit shelter. The forehead brace is wrapped in friction tape over reclaimed foam padding.

No two are identical. Chin straps are knotted cord or stripped wire depending on the maker's day. Acid-rain pitting marks every surface.

Slagside Scrapper's Half-Plate#

Built for the reclaimed industrial zones where the Shelf bleeds into active demolition corridors — places where falling debris, chemical runoff, and territorial disputes are all equally lethal. The foundation is a long-sleeve shirt in thick faded black synthetic, the kind of fabric that starts stiff and softens over years of wear; this one is soft. Over it, a sleeveless work jacket in rust-orange canvas has been armored with salvaged panel sections: the left shoulder carries a curved piece of hard composite cut from what was clearly once a vehicle door interior, strapped in place with three-point industrial webbing. The right shoulder is open — a deliberate choice, the straps there cut away to accommodate a chrome arm prosthetic that extends from just below the shoulder, matte-finished with the manufacturer's markings ground off, fingers worn smooth at the tips from use. The jacket's front is asymmetrically buttoned, the left side carrying six functioning cargo pockets, the right kept clear for arm movement. Trousers are combat-cut in worn olive, the thighs and shins reinforced with segments of rubber conveyor belt stitched over the original fabric, the knees blown out and repaired with self-repair tape that has yellowed and is beginning to peel at one edge. A thick belt in cracked brown synthetic leather carries a multi-tool in a molded holster, a small medical kit in a battered tin, and two more pockets whose contents make rectangular outlines under the flap. Boots are mid-calf, steel-reinforced at the toe, the right boot modified with a wider toe box to accommodate what looks like the beginning of a toe-chrome situation — a single augmented toe visible at the boot's open vamp when the laces are loose. A dented matte-black hard hat hangs from the belt by a clip, not worn, just carried.

Solberg-Maru Electrical Systems Crew Day Rig#

Solberg-Maru's electrical infrastructure crews are among the most aug-heavy workforces in the Circuit tier — chrome arms and neural-linked diagnostic ports are practically standard issue after three years on the job. This rig is designed around that reality. The primary garment is a flame-resistant work shirt in slate blue, rated for arc-flash exposure, with Solberg-Maru's double-helix-and-bolt logo embroidered in silver on the right chest and the worker's name patch in white on the left. The shirt has aug-accommodation construction along both sleeves: the inner seam runs on a magnetic-snap track that opens fully from shoulder to cuff, allowing a chrome arm to clear without the shirt being removed. A voltage-rated insulated over-vest in charcoal goes over the shirt — padded chest and back panels, flat front zip, and a broad rear pocket that accommodates a personal arc-flash shield in rolled form. The trousers are Fenmark ToughSeam-style in slate blue to match, with built-in knee pads, multiple tool pockets, and a reinforced gusset. Boots are Penrose Weld-style: broad-toe, steel-cap, dielectric-rated, with a side-zip for speed. A hard hat in Solberg-Maru yellow clips to the vest's back ring when not worn, and a pair of voltage-rated gauntlet gloves hang from a D-ring on the left hip. The ensemble is completed by a slim-profile BCI port cover in matte black — a snap-on shield that protects the worker's neural port from electrical field interference on high-voltage sites.

Solberg-Maru Fab Floor Technician's Rig#

The standard working dress of a mid-level fabrication floor technician at a Solberg-Maru manufacturing plant — one of the major Circuit employers running continuous production lines in M88's industrial eastern sectors. The centerpiece is a fitted coverall in deep charcoal grey synth-twill, single-piece construction with a heavy-gauge front zipper that runs from the left hip to the right shoulder in a diagonal — an ergonomic design that allows one-handed donning. The coverall has Solberg-Maru's angular teal-and-silver logo on the left chest and a name patch on the right reading in block letters. Sleeves are cut with extra fabric through the forearm for chrome arm accommodation and feature a secondary snap-seam from elbow to wrist that opens flat for workers with full prosthetic forearms. The back has a structured panel over the spine with magnetic attachment points for light exo-assist harness rigging. Knee pads are built-in hard-shell inserts with a quick-eject button on the outer knee.

Underneath the coverall, a long-sleeved moisture-wicking turtleneck in matte black keeps the neck and wrists protected from particulate. Safety boots are Solberg-Maru plant-standard: a matte charcoal composite-toe boot with a low heel, ESD-rated soles to prevent static discharge near sensitive fabrication equipment, and a wide-mouth tongue for easy on/off. The technician carries a tool belt worn over the coverall's exterior, a heavy nylon strap with modular snap-clip tool loops holding hex drivers, a calibration stylus, and a small diagnostic tablet in a rubberized holster. Safety glasses with teal-tinted lenses are pushed up on the forehead. Hair, if present, is tucked under a low-profile teal bump cap with the Solberg-Maru mark.
