Solberg-Maru Structural Maintenance Full Kit#

Solberg-Maru Infrastructure is one of the mid-tier corponations responsible for maintaining Meridian's aging transit tunnels, bridge superstructures, and elevated MagRail support columns — work that is unglamorous, physically demanding, and absolutely essential. Their field crew uniform is issued in two colors: charcoal grey for standard maintenance and safety orange for elevated-risk structural work. This kit is the standard grey issue. The coverall is a single-piece construction in heavy synth-canvas with articulated knees and elbows — pre-bent at the joint so the fabric doesn't bind when climbing or crouching — and a full-length front zipper backed by a magnetic snap storm flap. The Solberg-Maru logo, a stylized arch over a horizontal line (representing bridge over waterway), is heat-pressed in reflective silver on the back and left breast. A four-point harness anchor loop is reinforced into the upper back panel, rated to arrest a sixty-kilogram fall load. The collar is high and snug with a separate magnetic closure, designed to pair with a respirator mask that clips to a dedicated ring at the left collar point.

Underneath is an Ironpass Thermal Work Layer in dark charcoal, moisture-wicking and cut to allow full shoulder rotation. The boots are the Penrose Weld Boot, adapted here for climbing use with extra ankle support and a lug sole rated for rebar, grating, and wet concrete. A full-body tool harness in heavy nylon webbing goes over the coverall — carabiner points at both hips and the chest, with a tool-drop tether system for working at height. The hard hat is white Solberg-Maru branded with a pinned-on personal identification number and, almost always, at least one unauthorized sticker from a band, a political cause, or a neighborhood market. Aug-compatible at the spine and both shoulders: the coverall features a rear channel and bilateral shoulder zips that open cleanly for spinal rigs and shoulder-mounted chrome without compromising the structural integrity of the harness anchor. This is a rig for people who keep the city from falling down.

Solberg-Maru Thermal Work Layer#

Solberg-Maru makes workwear for people who spend time in cold industrial environments — the kind of cold that comes from unheated warehouses, exposed infrastructure catwalks, or the Lake Erie waterfront from November through April. Their thermal work layer is a fitted crew-neck shirt in brushed synthetic fleece-back jersey, designed to be worn under a jacket or hi-vis vest without bunching. The exterior is smooth enough to slide under outerwear; the interior is deeply brushed and traps heat efficiently. Reinforced panels run along the forearms and across the upper back — these areas get the most friction from tools, harnesses, and machinery.

Available in safety orange, slate, and a dark olive. No branding on the front — just a small woven label at the inside collar. The stitching at the cuffs is doubled and uses a stretch-resistant thread that doesn't fail when you're gripping something cold. This is a shirt that has never once been worn to a party and doesn't need to be.

Solenne Mirrorweave Bioluminescent Gala Gown#

Solenne's flagship gala gown is among the most recognized formal garments produced in Meridian 88, which is partly by design — it is meant to be seen and remembered. The foundation fabric is a proprietary mirrorweave silk-analog that shifts between deep iridescence and near-opacity depending on viewing angle and ambient light, creating the impression that the gown is made of something between water and metal. The hem is seeded with bioluminescent thread — a TESSERA-licensed biological compound woven directly into the fabric — that activates in low light and pulses with a slow, steady rhythm calibrated to approximate a resting heartbeat. The gown is fully custom-fitted via biometric scan and accommodates virtually any geneware modification — tail vents, wing slits, horn clearance at the neckline, and fur-friendly interior lining are all available as standard specifications. BCI-responsive color modulation allows the iridescent base to shift through a curated palette at the wearer's thought. A single gown of this type costs more than a Tier 2 resident earns in a year. This is not incidental to its design.

Solenne Mirrorweave Spire Gala Gown#

Solenne House does not advertise. It does not have a public address. Clients are introduced through existing clients, and the waiting period for a first consultation is measured in seasons. Their mirrorweave gown is the garment against which all other formal wear in Meridian 88 is implicitly measured, whether the people measuring it know the name or not. The fabric is a proprietary Solenne textile — holographic thread woven at a density that creates a surface which reflects and refracts light as if the gown is made of slow-moving water, shifting from silver to deep violet to colorless depending on viewing angle and ambient light source. The effect is not decorative. It is architectural. The gown does not fit into a room; it reorganizes the room around itself.

Beneath the holographic surface, the construction is a privacy-weave base layer that blocks passive biometric scanning, thermal imaging, and BCI handshake attempts — the Spire equivalent of discretion. Every closure, every seam, every accommodation for augmentation, geneware modification, or prosthetic is invisible from the outside. The gown has no visible openings because Solenne's atelier has hidden all of them so completely they don't read as openings at all. Price is not published. The Φ5,800 figure circulates as a floor estimate among Tier 4 observers who have never been in the same room as one.

Solenne Mirrorweave Spire Gala Suit#

A bespoke two-piece suit — or three-piece, or single-piece, depending on the commissioned configuration — woven from Solenne's proprietary mirrorweave fabric: a photonic thread structure that reflects the immediate environment in a slightly delayed, slightly abstracted way, so that the wearer appears to be wearing the room they're standing in. The effect is subtle at low settings and deeply disorienting at high. The suit's self-adjusting fit system uses a distributed microfilament network in the lining that reads the wearer's body temperature, posture, and movement and adjusts tension continuously, ensuring the garment never pulls, bags, or creases regardless of how the wearer moves. BCI-responsive color temperature allows the mirrorweave effect to be fine-tuned or disabled entirely from a thought-command.

Solenne produces fewer than forty suits per year. Each one is commissioned, fitted across three in-person sessions, and delivered in a case lined with the same mirrorweave fabric. The price includes lifetime alterations and a ten-year structural warranty. The suit can be built around any augment configuration and any geneware modification — Solenne's fitters are trained in anatomy that extends well beyond standard human. This is clothing as architecture, as argument, as the last word in any room.

Solenne's most exclusive nightlife offering sits at the intersection of biotechnology and haute couture, produced in runs of no more than twelve per season, each hand-finished to the client's specific genetic and augmentation profile. The foundation is a floor-length column gown in Solenne's proprietary Voidlace fabric — a living textile grown from bioluminescent algae cultures suspended in a nano-filament lattice, giving the fabric a deep black base that pulses with cold blue-white light in organic, non-repeating wave patterns that respond to the wearer's bioelectric field. No two pulse sequences are ever identical; the fabric reads as alive because it functionally is. The neckline is a deep architectural plunge at the front, with a dramatic open back that drops to the base of the spine, accommodating both spinal rig hardware and wing-bud geneware with a structured panel that frames rather than hides the hardware. For horn-bearing wearers, Solenne provides matching Voidlace horn wraps — strips of the same living fabric applied over genetic horn surfaces, making the horns pulse in sync with the gown. The column silhouette is broken only at the hip by a single asymmetric drape panel that falls open to the floor on the right side, revealing the leg beneath and accommodating tail geneware at the rear hip with an invisible pleat construction. Accessories are minimal by design: a single chrome cuff at the left wrist with a Solenne biosync chip that modulates the gown's pulse frequency in real time. Footwear is a custom platform sandal in grown-crystal resin, nearly translucent, catching the gown's bioluminescence and scattering it underfoot. In a dark room, the wearer appears to be standing inside light.

Solenne Voidspire Biolux Couture Night Set#

A Tier 5 Spire VIP lounge garment that costs more than most Shelf residents earn in a decade and wears that fact with perfect, terrifying calm. The core garment is a floor-length structured column dress in Solenne's proprietary Biolux silk — a living fabric grown from engineered silkworm geneware, each thread containing bioluminescent proteins that respond to the wearer's biometric state: heartbeat, emotional arousal, body temperature. A neural-port crown of brushed platinum and bioluminescent stone sits at the hairline: functional as a high-end BCI interface booster, worn as jewelry. Nothing is accidental. Nothing is cheap. Nothing announces its price.

Solstice Gear Packable Rain Shell#

A lightweight packable rain shell from Solstice Gear, a mid-market outdoor and urban-utility brand that does not pretend to be anything it is not. The jacket stuffs into its own chest pocket to form a palm-sized pouch, weighs almost nothing, and keeps rain out effectively for several hours before the seams begin to breathe. The fabric is a three-layer bonded nylon-polyester laminate with taped seams and a DWR-equivalent coating. Pit-zip vents. Adjustable hood with a single-hand cord lock. Available in high-vis yellow, slate, and a dark red that fades gracefully.

This is the jacket that lives in a bag until it is needed. Tier 2 workers who commute on foot, cyclists, delivery operators, and anyone who has been caught in a lake-effect storm without adequate gear owns or covets one. It is not stylish in any considered way. It is waterproof and it weighs nothing, which is its own kind of style.

Solvang Drift Parka#

Solvang is a Scandinavian-heritage outdoor brand that's been operating in the Great Lakes corridor for decades, selling gear to people who actually spend time outside in the region's serious winters. The Drift Parka is their cold-weather workhorse — a mid-thigh length shell in a matte ripstop with a down-analog synthetic fill, the hood oversized enough to accommodate a helmet or a heavy hat and still close around the face. The design is deliberately understated: two colors, glacier white and a dark navy, no visible branding beyond a small embossed logo at the chest zip. The insulation runs to the wrists and the fill weight is serious enough that below-zero temperatures feel like a negotiation rather than a defeat.

This is a Tier 3 to Tier 4 purchase — expensive enough that Tier 2 buyers make it a significant investment, cheap enough that it's not a status item in the Spire. Wilderness guides, researchers who work at the lake-monitoring stations, and people who commute via elevated walkways in January all wear it. It has none of the tech features of its more expensive competitors and doesn't need them. It is simply a very good parka.

Solvang Duster#

A knee-length to ankle-length duster in heavy waxed cotton canvas, cut generously through the shoulders and chest with a back split that runs from hem to mid-thigh for ease of movement. Solvang makes this coat in three lengths and four weights; the most popular is the mid-weight in tobacco brown or charcoal, with antique brass press-studs down the front and at the wrist adjusters. The lining is a printed flannel in a small geometric pattern — different every season, always muted. The wax finish gives the coat a slight sheen that develops a patina over years of wear, acquiring creases and darker marks at stress points that become part of the garment's character.

Solvang is a Tier 3 Norwegian-heritage label that has been in the corridor since the 2140s. The duster occupies a comfortable space between working coat and considered fashion — it reads differently depending on who's wearing it and where. On a Tier 3 professional it says deliberate; on a Tier 2 worker it says inherited or saved up for; on a geneware user with a tail or modified lower body it says practical, because the generous cut and back split accommodate anatomy that most coats don't. People who move through multiple zones in a day — fixers, journalists, independent contractors — favor it for exactly that reason.

Sootmark Nightwatch Layer Set#

Built for staying invisible in the dark industrial corridors of the Shelf while remaining functional in the cold. The base is a full-length thermal underlayer in matte black — the kind of utilitarian piece that Circuit-tier factories produce by the millions, here worn past its intended lifespan, the cuffs replaced with strips cut from a neoprene wetsuit and secured with adhesive seam tape. Over that comes a mid-layer hoodie in deep charcoal fleece, the hood reinforced with a wire brim salvaged from a hard hat so it holds its shape in wind without being pulled back. The hoodie's kangaroo pocket has been subdivided internally with sewn-in elastic loops holding a small flashlight, a multi-tool, and a folded strip of reflective tape for emergencies. The back panel has been stenciled in rust-colored paint with a crude geometric sigil, the mark of a specific Shelf block watch rotation. Trousers are slim-cut tactical in faded charcoal, both knees double-layered with iron-on rubber patches. Footwear is a pair of heavy low-profile boots in matte black rubber-composite, the lug soles worn almost flat but retreaded with adhesive grip strips along the ball of the foot for quiet movement on wet metal grating. A neck gaiter in dark gray sits around the throat, doubling as a face cover. Spinal rig aug-compatible: the jacket and hoodie both have a central back channel — a vertical seam left unstitched and finished with snap-close flaps — running from collar to hem.

Sorvaine Wing-Panel Cape#

Sorvaine is a small Tier 3-4 label that exists almost entirely to serve geneware users with wing modifications — a population that most mainstream outerwear manufacturers still design around rather than for. The Wing-Panel Cape is the brand's core offering: a structured cape with a full back panel that opens via a magnetic closure system running the length of the spine, allowing the garment to accommodate folded wings of varying spans without forcing the wearer to choose between being warm and being able to extend their modifications. The silhouette is dramatic and intentional — Sorvaine does not apologize for making something that reads as theatrical, because the people who need it have already accepted that their existence reads as theatrical to those who have not adapted.

Stratum Chrome-Vent Augment Specialist Set#

A Tier 4 specialist suit designed explicitly for heavily augmented workers who have grown tired of pretending their chrome doesn't exist. The jacket is a structured single-breasted cut in Stratum's 'Ironweave Coolform' — a matte dark slate fabric with a subtle crosshatch texture — tailored with open chrome-channel sleeves: both sleeves terminate at mid-forearm in a clean folded cuff with a wide magnetic-closure opening, designed so that chrome arms or prosthetic forearms can extend naturally without the fabric bunching or tearing. The channels are finished in exposed brushed steel binding that runs along the interior seam from shoulder to cuff, visible at the opening — a deliberate design choice that treats the augmentation as part of the silhouette rather than something to be hidden. The back panel has a reinforced spinal-rig dorsal channel: a structured spine of the jacket that accommodates external rig hardware, with three adjustment points that can be loosened via a side-access pull. The dress shirt beneath is a Stratum Executive Poplin in pale graphite with a standard cutaway collar, its sleeves cut short intentionally to sit at the bicep — the chrome-channel jacket cuff is meant to do the work from there.

Trousers are straight-cut Stratum Ironweave Coolform with a high rise and no break, worn with a slim brushed-steel-buckle belt. Footwear is the Crucible Chromestep Mid in matte black with steel cap, chosen for its visual echo of the chrome hardware at the wrists. The whole outfit leans into augmentation as aesthetic rather than hiding it — the chrome bindings, the open-channel cuffs, the spinal rig channel. This is someone who has stopped apologizing for their hardware and started treating it as a credential.

Stratum Executive Chrome-Panel Formal Suit#

Stratum's formal line for executive-tier employees is distinct from their standard corporate uniform output — this is a suit designed for representation, not function. Cut in a deep navy or charcoal wool-analog with a tight weave that reads as almost matte in daylight and slightly richer under interior lighting, the jacket features chrome-display panels along the upper lapels: small, polished insets that can be set to display a corponation logo, a tier-certification emblem, or left as mirror chrome. The panels connect to a small BCI-responsive module at the collar that allows the wearer to toggle display states with a thought. Augment-compatible shoulder and side seaming is standard.

This suit is what Stratum issues — or more precisely, what Stratum allows executives to purchase at a significant employee discount — when they need to represent the company at external events. It signals affiliation clearly and intentionally. The chrome panels catch the eye. That is the point. In rooms full of corporate formal wear, the display panel is a flag.

Stratum Executive Formal Dress Uniform#

Stratum's formal dress uniform is issued to management-tier employees for client presentations, regulatory appearances, and internal advancement ceremonies. The jacket is structured worsted synth-wool in deep charcoal with a subtle herringbone weave visible only in direct light. Rank insignia is embedded in the left breast in Stratum's standard chromatic thread — color-shifting from silver to gold depending on seniority level, verified by a micro-NFC chip that can be scanned at security checkpoints. The trousers are cut with a full-break hem and include a hidden cable-management channel along the left inner seam for BCI tether routing.

The uniform is not sold — it is issued, registered to the employee's ID, and must be returned upon separation from the company. Employees who leave Stratum under good terms receive a certificate allowing them to purchase the uniform at cost (Φ140). Employees separated for cause have the uniform remotely flagged — the chromatic thread shifts to a flat gray that doesn't respond to light, which is not subtle.

Stratum Executive Poplin#

A dress shirt engineered for the Tier 4 corporate environment: crisp white poplin weave with a subtle self-stripe visible only in direct light, spread collar, French cuffs, and a back yoke cut to allow full range of motion without pulling. The fabric is a high-thread-count synthetic-cotton blend that resists wrinkling through a twelve-hour shift and repels minor liquid contact — coffee, rain — without any active tech. Just tight weave and a surface finish applied at the mill.

The Stratum logo appears on the interior collar only — a small embossed mark. No external branding. The shirt is designed to look anonymous and expensive at the same time, which is exactly what Tier 4 professionals want. It is the default dress shirt of three separate corponation administrative dress codes, worn under suit jackets or alone with the sleeves rolled at after-hours client dinners.

Stratum Logistics Warehouse Operations Uniform#

Stratum supplies warehouse and logistics operations across Meridian 88's distribution network, and their standard warehouse operations uniform is the daily reality for tens of thousands of workers in the city's fulfillment centers, sorting hubs, and cold-storage facilities. The set consists of a reinforced polo shirt, cargo trousers with articulated knees, a high-visibility safety vest, and an optional thermal liner for cold-chain facilities. The polo and trousers come in company-specific colorways — employers purchase branded versions with their own logo over-printed on the Stratum base — but the cut and construction are standardized. The safety vest is the item with the most technology: embedded in the hi-vis panels are passive RFID nodes that interface with warehouse management systems, logging worker location, task completion, and equipment interaction without requiring active input.

The trousers feature a full tool-loop array at the thigh and hip, sized for handheld scanners, stylus tools, and packing materials. Knee panels are reinforced with gel-core impact absorption for workers who spend time crouching at lower rack levels. Augment compatibility is handled through a universal port-access panel system on the forearms and a back panel with breakaway seams for dorsal chrome. Geneware tail accommodations are standard on all Stratum trousers. Workers generally receive two sets per year and are responsible for their own maintenance — a point of ongoing friction in Stratum-supplied workplaces, as the sets degrade faster than the replacement cycle accounts for.

Stratum MagLine Transit Operator Day Rig#

A sharp, company-issued uniform built for transit operators running M88's elevated rail and underground tube lines. The core is a structured navy polyblend jacket with Stratum Logistics' orange-and-grey chevron shoulder patch stitched directly into the seam — not ironed on, not going anywhere. The jacket has a mandarin collar, snap-close breast pockets, and a left-chest embroidered name panel in block lettering. Underneath sits a moisture-wicking charcoal thermal base layer with a half-zip neck, designed to regulate body temperature through platform heat surges and cold tunnel drafts. Trousers are navy cargo-cut with reinforced knees, two side cargo pockets sealed with magnetic closures, and a low-profile tool loop on the right thigh for fare scanner holsters or comms clips. A hi-vis orange stripe runs the outer leg seam — retro-reflective in low light. Boots are the Veldtmann Steelcap 7 equivalent construction: thick rubber composite sole, steel toe cap, ankle support wrap, and oil-resistant tread. A charcoal knit watch cap with a small Stratum emblem on the cuff finishes the head. The whole kit reads institutional but maintained — pressed enough to mean the wearer takes the job seriously, worn enough to mean they've been doing it for years.

Stratum Mid-Grade Analyst's Pressed Set#

Stratum Mid-Grade Pressed Occasion Set#

The Tier 3 worker's best effort, worn to presentations, performance reviews, and the occasional internal ceremony they were not expecting to attend. The Stratum Mid-Grade Pressed Occasion Set is a two-piece suit in medium charcoal poly-blend — not cheap enough to be embarrassing, not fine enough to be mistaken for something better. Footwear is a pair of Stratum-brand matte-black derby shoes, adequate in construction, resoled once at a street cobbler. The entire ensemble was purchased at a Stratum corporate outlet and comes with a two-year 'professional appearance guarantee,' which is a warranty no one has ever successfully claimed. Strikeshield Dynamics BDA-9 Blast Disposal Suit#

Bulky, olive-drab full-body blast attenuation suit with articulated composite panels over a shear-thickening fluid underlayer. The outer shell is matte-finished boron carbide over polycarbonate, with a distinctive quilted appearance from the fluid-pack underlayer beneath. SwiftRoute Last-Mile Delivery Uniform Set#

SwiftRoute's last-mile delivery drivers cover every tier of Meridian 88, from Shelf drop-offs to Spire concierge delivery, and their uniform reflects that range of environments. The set includes a weathershell jacket in SwiftRoute's cobalt blue with retroreflective silver trim on the shoulders, chest, and cuffs for visibility in low-light urban conditions; a moisture-wicking base-layer shirt; and reinforced cargo trousers with expandable knee panels for riders who spend shifts on electric cargo bikes. The jacket is waterproof to IP68 standard and rated for sustained operation in M88's frequently severe weather corridors along the lake. GPS routing hardware is woven into the left sleeve in a mesh antenna pattern that feeds directly to the driver's BCI delivery overlay.

The uniform is designed for constant motion: every closure is magnetic or snap-based for one-handed operation, and the collar seals quickly against weather without requiring both hands. Port-access panels are integrated at the left wrist for BCI scanning hardware used to authenticate deliveries. The jacket back panel is split-vent for geneware-modified riders with tail modifications, and the collar is sized generously for workers with neck or jaw augmentation. SwiftRoute drivers are tracked continuously via the GPS mesh; the uniform is, functionally, a monitoring device. Most drivers know this and have made their peace with it, or haven't.

Tarnveil Biolum Suppression Operative Rig#

Designed explicitly for runners carrying bioluminescent geneware — the subdermal glow, luminous patterning, or light-emitting scales that are fashionable in 2200 but catastrophically conspicuous on a night job. A pair of thin suppression gloves in matching olive is stored in the inside chest pocket, extending coverage to the hands. The complete set, worn and closed, reduces visible bioluminescence to near zero in practical field conditions.

TESSERA BioOps Field Suit — Class 3#

TESSERA's security personnel don't look like traditional corpsec. The BioOps Field Suit is constructed from a living mycoweave — a textile threaded with engineered fungal filaments that respond to environmental biohazard markers. When the suit detects airborne pathogens, engineered retrovirals, or unauthorized geneware trigger compounds, the mycoweave tightens its pore structure to near-impermeability and signals through a soft bioluminescent pulse along the collar seam. The exterior is a pale, clinical white with TESSERA's double-helix emblem rendered in raised stitching at the left breast. The suit is designed to be visually non-threatening — TESSERA's field presence is as much about information gathering and specimen recovery as enforcement.

The BioOps suit includes sealed specimen-pouch integration along the thigh and forearm, and the hood assembly can be raised and sealed to the collar with a single gesture command through BCI integration. Because TESSERA operatives frequently interact with geneware subjects — willing and otherwise — the suit is engineered with wide geneware accommodation: tail clearance, dorsal slitting for early-stage wing configurations, and horn-clearance headgear options. The living mycoweave requires quarterly maintenance at a TESSERA service node to remain fully functional, creating ongoing dependency on TESSERA infrastructure.

TESSERA BioOps Lab Technician Coverall#

Issued to TESSERA's bench-level geneware technicians working in BSL-2 and BSL-3 environments, this full-body coverall is constructed from a microporous film laminate that blocks particulates, aerosolized biologicals, and most common chemical splashes. The exterior is TESSERA's clinical white with a subtle helix-pattern emboss visible only under UV — a mark of authenticity that prevents counterfeit uniforms from entering secure lab areas. Integrated hood and booties attach via sealed magnetic closures. Disposable in theory, but most techs wash and reuse them until the laminate integrity fails, typically at around 30 cycles.

The suit is designed with the full range of TESSERA's own geneware modifications in mind — there are discrete fin-shaped vents along the spine for bioluminescent skin that can overheat under sealed suits, and the hood has a structured internal frame to accommodate horn clearance up to 18cm. A wrist-mounted contamination sensor logs exposure events and syncs to the wearer's BCI. The suit does not accommodate external chrome augmentation well; workers with significant cyberware typically request custom-cut versions at additional cost, which TESSERA docks from their pay.

Vantablack Formal Liaison Suit — Nullsignal Cut#

Not available through any civilian or commercial channel, the Nullsignal Cut is Vantablack's formal wear option for personnel who attend diplomatic, legal, or inter-corponation events in an official liaison capacity. The fabric is a proprietary weave that absorbs approximately 94% of visible light, creating an effect that reads as depth rather than color — the suit does not look black so much as it looks like an absence. Under standard interior lighting it is striking. Under low light it becomes difficult to visually track. The cut is conventional formal — two-button, notched lapel — which makes the visual effect more unsettling rather than less. Privacy-weave lining blocks biometric scanning at standard commercial sensor ranges.

The suit carries no visible Vantablack branding. It carries no visible anything. That is the design brief. Vantablack personnel attending formal functions are not there to be identified. They are there to observe, to represent an interest that prefers not to be named in the room, and to leave without being clearly described afterward.

Vantablack Internal Security Analyst Uniform#

Vantablack's internal security analysts do not carry weapons in the conventional sense. Their uniform reflects this: it is designed to communicate authority through absence rather than display. The suit is constructed from a matte-black fabric with a light-absorption coefficient high enough to make the wearer appear slightly two-dimensional in photographs and low-resolution surveillance footage — a practical choice that doubles as a psychological tool. The cut is slim and precise, with no external pockets, no visible fasteners, and no brand markings of any kind. A Vantablack analyst's uniform is identified by what it lacks.

The fabric incorporates passive signal-dampening threads that reduce the wearer's BCI broadcast signature without fully masking it — enough to prevent casual eavesdropping, not enough to trigger the anti-spoofing protocols in secure facilities. Wrist cuffs contain embedded haptic nodes that allow encrypted tap-communication between team members in environments where verbal or digital communication is inadvisable. The uniform is issued as a complete set and must be returned on reassignment; analysts who attempt to retain theirs are contacted once, politely, and the matter is resolved without further documentation.

Vantablack Operations Thermal Coat#

A long insulated coat issued to Vantablack field personnel operating in cold-weather or extended outdoor conditions. The shell is a matte charcoal ripstop with a subtle corponation identifier woven into the collar lining — not a logo, just a thread pattern that reads under UV. Filled with a thin but highly effective synthetic insulation, the coat is warm without the bulk that would restrict movement or make it harder to access sidearms or equipment. Two deep hand pockets, a zippered chest pocket, and a sealed interior document pocket.

This coat signals Vantablack in a way that the average person recognizes without being able to articulate why. It's not branded. It's just cut a certain way, in a certain color, with a certain quality of fabric, worn by people who move with a certain economy. On the Shelf, seeing this coat means getting out of the way. In Tier 4 corridors, it means a meeting is happening that you're not part of.

Vantablack Ops Liaison Jacket#

Vantablack doesn't issue tactical uniforms in the traditional sense. The Ops Liaison Jacket is designed to look like civilian outerwear — a trim, mid-length coat in flat matte black that reads as expensive street fashion until it doesn't. The exterior fabric is woven with Vantablack's signature light-absorption compound, not to the extreme of true VantaMat applications, but enough to make the wearer visually recede in low-light environments, reducing silhouette definition and making optical tracking systems struggle for clean acquisition. The jacket carries no visible corporate branding; the only identifying marker is a microscopic spectral tag in the left cuff, readable only by Vantablack-issued scanners.

Internally, the jacket is a different garment entirely. A network of sensor-filament threads maps the wearer's immediate environment and feeds data through a BCI port concealed within the collar seam. Pockets are shielded against RF scanning, and the lining includes a signal-dampening mesh that limits the wearer's electronic signature in monitored spaces. The jacket is cut to read as civilian across Tier 3 through 5 environments — it is not designed for the Shelf, where anyone wearing something that expensive without obvious corp affiliation becomes a target. Vantablack personnel who operate in lower tiers are typically issued cover garments to wear over the jacket. Possession without authorization is deeply inadvisable.

Vantablack Signals Intelligence Analyst Suit#

Vantablack's internal SIGINT analysts don't wear tactical gear — they wear this. A precisely cut two-piece suit in a deep charcoal so dark it reads as near-black under most lighting, constructed from a wool-silk blend woven with passive EM shielding thread that reduces the wearer's electronic emissions signature without requiring active counter-measure hardware. The jacket's lining contains a thin Faraday mesh layer that blocks short-range BCI interrogation — the kind of passive scanning common in Tier 4 and 5 lobbies. No logo, no branding. The only identifying mark is a small VB stamp on the interior collar tag, visible only when you know to look.

The suit is tailored to order for each analyst and replaced on a 12-month cycle regardless of condition — Vantablack considers the wear pattern on a suit to be identifying information. Augmentation accommodation is handled at the tailoring stage: port access panels, chrome shoulder clearance, and geneware adjustments are cut individually and documented only in the analyst's classified personnel file. Wearing this suit outside Vantablack business contexts is not prohibited, but analysts are quietly counseled against it. The suit has no public retail existence.

Vantablack Signals Security Escort Uniform#

Vantablack's escort security operatives occupy a different role than their analyst counterparts — they are physically present, visible, and intended to project a specific kind of deterrence. Their uniform reflects this: a structured black jacket over matching tactical trousers, with a matte-finish chest rig that carries no visible weapon mounts but has hardpoints rated for rapid attachment of Vantablack-issued equipment. The jacket's fabric incorporates the same light-absorption weave used in analyst suits, making the wearer appear slightly flattened in recording environments — useful when accompanying clients who require discretion about their security arrangements. A single white Vantablack sigil — the only visible branding — is set into the left collar in reflective thread visible only under direct light.

The chest rig is the operationally significant element. Its front panels are layered with soft armor rated for standard ballistics, and the rear panel carries a signal-isolation membrane that provides limited protection against directed-energy BCI disruption — a threat taken seriously in Vantablack's operational environment. The uniform is sized and cut to accommodate significant augmentation; the jacket back has a full-length magnetic closure panel for operatives with extensive dorsal chrome, and sleeve lengths are available in extended cuts for arm-augmented personnel. Geneware accommodations are not standard issue — Vantablack's escort division maintains strict physical specifications that functionally exclude most significant geneware modifications, a policy that has generated quiet external criticism and internal legal review.

Vanthorpe Analyst's Quiet Distinction Set#

A Tier 4 specialist's daily armor — the suit that says 'I earn more than you think but I'm not stupid enough to show it.' The jacket is a single-breasted two-button cut in Vanthorpe's 'Selvedge Coolweave' — a structured synth-wool blend with a faint herringbone texture visible only in direct light, in a color called 'graphite dusk' that reads as charcoal in fluorescent office lighting and almost navy near windows. The lapels are slightly wider than the Tier 3 standard issue, a meaningful signal in corporate fashion. Interior pockets are aug-compatible with a reinforced chrome-arm channel sewn along the left sleeve lining, factory-finished with clean bias binding. The dress shirt beneath is a Vanthorpe Coolweave Dress Shirt in pale sand, with a proper spread collar and genuine button closures — no magnetic shortcuts. Trousers are the matching Selvedge Coolweave in graphite dusk, with a proper full break and a discreet side-adjusting waistband that accommodates the slight postural shifts of a spinal rig without bunching.

Footwear is a Fenwick Monk-Strap in cognac leather-analog, polished to a shine that required deliberate effort. A slim brushed-titanium watch on the left wrist — not a smart device, pointedly analog — and a single dark-metal ring on the right hand. No lanyard. The badge is kept in a slim cardholder in the breast pocket, produced only when necessary. The whole ensemble costs roughly eight times what a comparable Tier 3 set costs, and looks approximately twice as good — the gap in visible quality deliberately understated. This person knows the rules well enough to bend them without breaking them.

Vanthorpe Coolweave Dress Shirt#

Vanthorpe's answer to the problem of looking composed in a city that runs hot and humid eight months a year. The Coolweave is a spread-collar dress shirt in a micro-vented poplin — the weave is tight enough to look crisp in a meeting but open enough at the fiber level to wick and breathe. Available in white, pale blue, chalk grey, and a warm ecru. The buttons are matte synthetic shell, the placket is fused for flatness, and the back has a single box pleat for movement.

This is the shirt a Tier 3 professional reaches for when they have something important to do. It doesn't wrinkle badly, it photographs well, and it sits in the middle of the price range where you're not showing off but you're clearly not skimping. Vanthorpe's corporate line gets a lot of eye rolls, but the Coolweave earns its place in the drawer.

Vanthorpe Meridian Blazer#

Vanthorpe's answer to the question of what a corporate professional wears when the meeting isn't formal enough for a suit but casual isn't acceptable. The Meridian Blazer is a single-breasted two-button in a medium-weight wool-poly blend available in charcoal, navy, and a dark forest that reads almost black in poor light. The construction is half-canvassed — more structure than a dress blazer, less than a suit jacket — and the lapels are a modest notch cut that doesn't date quickly. Interior pockets are deep and numerous, a Vanthorpe signature. The lining is a deep burgundy silk-analog that shows only when the jacket opens.

This is the jacket that Tier 3 professionals live in. It goes over a dress shirt for a client meeting and over a henley for a working lunch. It's been carefully designed to communicate that the wearer is serious without being ostentatious, which is exactly the register that Tier 3 corporate culture requires. Tier 4 buyers occasionally pick it up as a casual alternative to their bespoke pieces. It is not an exciting jacket. It is a jacket that works every day for years.

Vanthorpe Voidcut Chrome Reveal Suit#

A Tier 4 club and lounge outfit that exists at the exact intersection of corporate authority and deliberate transgression — the kind of suit that reads as professional from across the room and as something more dangerous up close. The jacket is single-button, structured, in deep midnight-blue synth-wool with a subtle self-pattern woven in near-black reactive thread that shifts geometry slowly — so slowly it takes several minutes of observation to confirm it's moving. The lapels are faced in mirror-chrome synth-leather, and the jacket's interior lining is holographic silver, visible as the wearer moves. Both sleeves terminate at the elbow in engineered cutoffs — clean, deliberate, chrome-edged — leaving the forearm fully exposed: for wearers with chrome augmentation this frames the hardware precisely; for those without it reads as equally intentional minimalism. A fitted high-collar shirt underneath is sheer black with a structured front placket, the collar designed with a wide notch at the back for neural port access. Trousers are slim, midnight-blue synth-wool matching the jacket, with a single holographic silver stripe down each outer seam that activates under UV. Heavy-duty work gloves in charcoal nitrile-coated synth-leather hang clipped to a D-ring at the hip. The whole kit reads worn but maintained: clean at shift start, grimy by shift end, and built to survive both.

Veldtmann Pressline Hi-Vis Safety Shell#

A class-3 high-visibility safety jacket in fluorescent yellow-green with retroreflective silver tape across the chest, back, and sleeves in a segmented pattern. The outer shell is a coated polyester that resists light chemical splash and wipes clean with a damp cloth. Veldtmann is the same Tier 1-2 workwear manufacturer known for their assembly line kits — this shell is issued to port workers, construction crews, waste management staff, and anyone working near moving machinery or vehicle traffic.

There is nothing fashionable about this jacket. It is a safety garment. It does its job: it makes the wearer visible in low light and bad weather from a significant distance. Some Shelf-district residents wear them off-shift because they're free or near-free through employer issue, because they're warm enough, or because — in certain neighborhoods — being visibly dressed as a worker provides a specific kind of social camouflage that keeps you from being hassled.

Veldtmark Splitpanel Night Operative Set#

A night-work rig that refuses the all-black cliché with conviction — this ensemble is built in deep navy and weathered wine-red, colors that disappear in M88's sodium-tinged nighttime streetlight better than black ever does against artificial illumination. Trousers are straight-cut in charcoal anthracite with a scanner-resistant weave, carrying six total pockets — two standard, two deep thigh with mag-close, and two hidden rear waistband pockets. Footwear is a mid-calf boot in dark oxblood synthetic leather with a stacked composite heel that adds two centimeters of height — a subtle silhouette change that confounds gait-recognition systems — and a hollow heel compartment sized for a data chip stack or a folded emergency med-patch.

Verath & Lund Birdseye Sweater#

A crewneck sweater knitted in a traditional birdseye pattern — small, repeating two-color diamond checks — from Verath & Lund's house merino-cashmere blend. The yarn is sourced from a cooperative in what was once Patagonia and processed at V&L's mill in the upper Great Lakes corridor. The result is a sweater with genuine weight and presence: it holds its shape, repels light moisture, and softens over time rather than pilling. Colors come in pairs — the birdseye is always two tones, typically a neutral ground with a darker check, or occasionally an unexpected pairing like sage and burgundy.

Verath & Lund occupies a strange position in Meridian 88's fashion landscape — they're not fashionable, exactly, but they are respected. The Birdseye Sweater is something a Tier 3 professional might inherit from a parent or save up for deliberately, wear for fifteen years, and eventually hand off again. It sits equally well in a Tier 3 apartment and at a Tier 4 casual gathering. It is the sweater of people who buy things once.

Verath & Lund Lambswool Crewneck#

Verath & Lund has been making knitwear in the Scandinavian-minimalist tradition since the 2140s, and the Lambswool Crewneck is as close to a house signature as the brand gets — a simple, clean silhouette in a mid-weight lambswool blend that they source from a single cooperative farm in what used to be Norway. The neck is a true crew, not too high and not too wide, and the body is slightly relaxed without being oversized. It comes in a restrained palette: oatmeal, slate, charcoal, and one seasonal color each year (2199 was a dusty rose that sold out in ten days).

The fabric has a slight texture to it — not scratchy, but present. You know you're wearing wool. It pills slightly after heavy use, which Verath & Lund addresses with a complimentary depilling service at their boutiques. The sweater is the kind of thing that gets worn for fifteen years and still looks considered. Tier 3 and Tier 4 buyers make up most of the market. It requires hand washing or a gentle cycle with cold water and the appropriate bag, and the care instructions are printed on a small woven label inside the left hem in both Norwegian and Standard.

Wetwall Night Crawler's Stealth Wrap#

Everything about this outfit is built around moving through the Shelf after dark without being seen, heard, or remembered. The foundation is a skin-close base layer in dark navy, barely distinguishable from black, in a moisture-wicking weave that's been hand-dyed unevenly — the dye job is amateur but effective, breaking up any reflective sheen. Over that: a long-sleeved pullover in matte dark gray, the neck cut low and wide enough to pull up over the nose, the cuffs long enough to cover the wrists entirely. The outer layer is a deconstructed hooded jacket, its original shape somewhere between a coach's shell and a rain anorak, now cut down, re-seamed, and fitted with a series of interior pockets accessible through hidden slits — one at the chest, two at the lower hem, one inside each sleeve near the wrist. The hood is deep and can be cinched to a narrow oval around the face. The whole jacket is treated with a matte-finish waterproofing compound that kills any surface sheen. Trousers are slim-fit in heavy black cotton twill, the inner ankle seams reinforced with self-repair tape to prevent snagging. Boots are soft-soled, mid-ankle, in worn synthetic suede that's been re-dyed black — near-silent on most Shelf flooring, with a thin but grippy rubber sole. Thin knit gloves in charcoal complete the set. There is nothing reflective anywhere on this outfit. No hardware, no exposed metal, no pale thread.
